_ ANOT HER YEAR. Another year has dawned on human life, Yet evil passions keep the world in strife; O'er our, dear sister isle_the elouds hang low, _ And better times in coming seem too slow. Why are the dreams of poeti inientoved? Why is the happiness of life destroyed?, Is it because the subtle power of sin- as blighted lovely, tender joys that-spring Within the heart, where, Struggling for the light, Affection pure oft meets with error's blight ?- • early flowers, though fated in their kVA. • • Yet beautil y the cold and barren earth, Tell us the wintry storms are fleeting by. And cheer our spirits we they droop and die— The first sweet tokens of _returning spring, That make the pairing birds in gladness sing— So love end friendshipcheer life's chequered day, And truthful honour is not cast away. When gentle showers the balmy zephyrs blow, And washirOm lofty hills the winter's snow, More numerous buds bedeck the lively green. And spring is in her maiden beauty aeon ' The gin's director and more friendly ray- • Soon drives the chilly morning *lnds Away: And summer breathes upon the flowers that stray Wild in their beauty on a sunny day. From scenes progressive in this circling splere Take hope that man shall be more happy be; ; Hope and be *aye, the gloom upon thy twow. If wrought by doubt. should vanish civen now. Though selfishness and error give thee pain, Yet friendship, trutk. and love are not in vain. Ali, could we in tidy year so young and new In all one actions be snore lost and trne, Avoid the causes front whence sorrows flow, 7,1 And peaceful pleasure in its passing know; Then we might hope thit future years shall be From errors and from troubles past more free. With joyful plenty, may this land be blest, From 8.1,X10111 cares her toiling people rest; And temperance regulate a better day, And her rich blessings with the people 'stay! May poverty and crime grow less each year, -Till, lost in happiness, they disappear .1 Oh, happiness mankind have known in part, And dimly seen how beautiful thou art, Affection shines within thy beaming eyes • Like brightest stars through all the azulre skies No wrinkles on thy perfect face are seen, For peace within thy heart bath ever been; Ty nature cams& to temptations bow, Nor anxious thonghts e'er cross thy peaceful brow. Discord can ne'er possess thy tranquil breast, Nor evil prrssions e'er disturb thy rest; Revenge and malice thou eanst never know, Blessings attend whdre'er thy footsteps go. • From error, selfishness, and sorrow free. Viee and injustice have no part in thee' For thou art noble and divine of race, Oh lead us to thy radiant dwelling-Place! • • S. KaltlON, Warrington.

AN OLD BACKELOR'S COMPLAINT. I'm tired of hearing about " • Of Christdias, and New-tear's Day I'm a prudent, careful man,-yet still -' For others' folryi pay. It's been "give" for this, for that, and there, And "giving," and "giving," everywhere,. There i 4 -Lazarus always at my gate, • For clothing or for rations: • " My brother," indeed! and if he were, ' I don't blow poor relations. They say, " He is hungry, and must be fed: Let the proper quarters give him bread. • All the year roun.d it is bad enough, But it's worse at Christmas-tide . Then if a man is not stern and gruff. 'He'll be-robbed on every side. ' 'tor trees, and trash, and this and that feed, ,Thatl'm very sure the poor don't need. I pay my way-, and I never crave A favour from any man ; Yet eveiy serving-lass and knave— Uaria. John, and Dan— Has thought mv pocket-book /awful prey, i Because, forsooth, t is Christmas-day! 'Tis true I hire saved a million or so, But I have myself to thank; And if! gave like some men-I know, - Where would I be with my bank? It's nonsense, and idleness, eery way, This keeping of Christmas holiday.

Don't mind shitering on the bank' but Pitch rite in and stick your head under and shiver it out Thar ai • n't any more trick in getting married than there is in eating, Peanuts. Many a man has stood ehivering on the shore until the river run out. Don't ex- pect to marry an angel—they have all been picked out long ago. Remember, Joe, you ain't a sam" t yourself. Do not marry for beauty exclusively; beauty is 'like ice, awfully eippery, and thaws dreadfully easy Don't mar for Inv' neither; buy is like a cooking-seon* good for nothing when the fuel gives out. But let the mixture be some beauty, becomingly dressed, with about set° in her pocket, a good speller, handy and neat in her house, plenty of good sense, tuff constitution and by-laws, small feet, a light step; add to this a warm heart and sound teeth. The mixture will keep in any climate and will not evaporate. Don't marry tor pedigree, unless it's backed by bank-notes. A family with nothing but pedigree generally lacks sense.

TIM INDIAN IMPORT DunES.—DHPVITATIONI TO THE 111AnQUIS OF HARTINOTON.—The influential deputation from Lancasfiire waited upon the Marquis of Hartington, on Wednesday, at the India Office. on the subject of the Indian , cotton import duties. Mr. Briggs, M.P., introduced the de- putation, and pointed out the embarrassing position in which the Lancashire trade was placed by the existicg arrangements, and the disagreeable and capricious way in which the Custom-house duties were performed. The mem- bers of the deputation urged that the entire remission of the duties on grey goods would be the greatest benefit which could be conferred upon Lancashire. Mr. Raynsford Jack- son submitted that there should be an appeal from the de- cisions of collectors of customs, who under the existing ar- rangements had the power of imposing heavy fines. In reply, Lord Hartington hoped the inconveniences complained of would have the effect of convincing the Government of India that the present system was one which could not be permanently maintained, but that they must go forward and not backward. The Home Government felt strongly that whatever remedies might have to be applied to remove the jpconveniences which prevailed they would not revert to the old policy, but they must take the form of greater freedotn to the trade. On this question he was entirely prepared to adopt the policy bequeathed to him by his predecessors, Lord Salisbury and Lord Cranbrook, and he believed Lord Ripon was prepared to adopt the policy of Lord Lytton and , Sir John Strachey. As soon as the finances of India would allow, he should be prepared to proceed further in the same direction. He felt that a retrogide liter) was impossible, I and the practical suggestions made by the deputation should receive the earliest and most careful attention of the Govern-

ALLBGBD "BOYCOTTIBD" me ENGLAND.-011 Monday, at the Cockermouth Police Court, a young man named James Bradley was charged with having wounded William M'Quin, flax dresser, of Cockermouth, on Christmas Eve. The Prisoner had gone into prosecutorThouse and said he was "Boycotted." Prosecutor asked him who had done that, to which prisoner replied the men in the shop. Prosecutor said they would not have done that for nothing. Prisoner asked him if he would "Boycott" him too, and he replied, "Whatever my shop mates do, I will do the same." Prose- cutor saw there was likely to be a row, and he got up to put the prisoner out. A scuffle took place, in which both men fell to the floor. Eventually Bradley was got outside, and on coming in and sitting down the prosecutor found blood running down his clothes from a wound in his neck, and called out to a man in the house that he was stabbed. Dr. Dodgson wall called in, and found a wound in the prosecu- tor's throat from one and a half to two inches long, but not deep, just along the prominent part of the throat. The wound bl&I freely. The prisoner was committed for trial at the Cumberland assizes.

Tan AFFILIATION QFASTION,—At the Liverpool Police] Court, on Tuesday, Mr. Raffles, the stipendiary magistrate, gave an important decision in reference to an atDliation question which is at present, from a legal point of view, in I doubt. Last week, Mary Finnegan summoned Richard Ilessan, a clothier carrying on business in Liverpool, to recover ten weeks' arrears, under an order made some years ago in respect of his illegitimate child. Mr. Murphy appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Copeman for the defendant. The ground, as stated by Mr. Copeman, on which the defendant refused to pay was that the complain- ant had been and was at present married. The magistrates had, until a recent decision, held that the marriage of the mother of the child required no further payment on the part 1 of the father, but now it appeared that there was a question about the matter. Mr. Raffles adjourned the case, as being Most important, to consider the point of law. He now gave his decision against the defendant, that the marriage of the mother was no bar to the claim for the support of thechi by the father, in as made by the magistrates the order d affiliation. FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
-DISXSTER-TO-BICTISH`TIODPS TitrlCS: veer,. _ It is placed liefottd cklubtAhat a -detachment of the 94t.h

Regiment was stirprise,d by the -Boers on Monday week, oh the march from Leydenberg to Pretoriapa distance of 200 miles, with the disastrous result of 120 Britisk soldiers killed and wounded and 37 taken prisoners. The colours of the regiment were saved. Sir G. Colley, the officer commansling in Natal, in reporting the disaster to the War Office; asks for a cavalry regiment to be sent to him quickly, He feels that the overpowering of the British detachment will ,materially alter the situation, as it will encourage the Boers, who will now also feel themselves committed. On Sunday- it was decided,to send out to Natal the 6th (Inniskilling) Dragoons, now stationed at Norwich. Arrangements are being pushed forward at the ordasnce stores at Woolwich for seniing im- mediate supplies te the Cape. ' , ' Further details of the disaster 'to tritish troops tam week in the Transvaal have been telegraphed from Durban, and it is made clear that the massacre was due to a "surprise," , and that the war will be of a most bitter character. It ap- pears that the moment of attack selected was favourable to the Boers, as it was just at the time an 'effort was being made to extricate the waggons of the 94th llogiment from a swamp, and when Lieutenant Colonel Anstruther and his handful of men had, in. order to render aasistince, laid aside their arms: "'Upon the appearance of the Boers the soldiers rushed to their weapons, but before they conld place them- selves in a defensive position they were shot down by their assailants. It is reported from-Kimberley in four Eaglish- men have been murdered in cold blood n the midst of an assembly of 3,000 Boers. The driver of a postcart, has also been murdered and his mail bags carried' off. There is a re- port that Colonel Bellaire has shelled the Boers out of Potchefstroom, killing 100 and wounding many. Through- out the Transvaal the wildest excitement prevails. At home arrangements have been made for the despatch of a regiment of cavalry and a battery of artillery to Natal, and a Reuter's telegram says that on- Monday the Tamar left Gibraltar with the 97th Regiment for Capetown and Natal. • An unsuccessful attempt has been made to cat off the cattle of the rebels in the ',tribe district. On December 20, Colonel Carrington was still patrolling in Basutoland. Dunnes, Tuesday.—A portion of the mail from the TritiaViud has arrived.,-Letters state that the first shot of the war was fired at Potchefstroom, by order of Major Clarke, upon a body of armed Boers approaching the military camp. Commandant Cronje was killed sad five Boers wounded. This is said to have been the actual corn-, mencement of hostilities.—The town of Potchefstriom is now hi the hands of the Boers, who are said to be 6,000 strong. At Heidelberg there are 3,000 of them. As Sir Pomeroy Colley will he escorted to Newcastle by the newly- arrived drafts, the services of the volunteers called out for that purpose will now not be required. Carrrows, December 24.—The postal line between this and the Transvaal has been entirely. idterrupted, and for twelve days no letters have come 'through. From Kimber- ley we have conflicting accounts of what is going on, but you will be better informed in England than we are here. The excitement is great, and the 91st are in readiness to embark for Durban at the shortest notice.—ln Basutoland there is no change. Colonel Carrington has returned to Mateteng, having effected nothing.—ln Caffreland the Pondomise have been beaten in several encounters by Colonel Baker's force.—General Clarke is still at Umtata.

BERLIN, Wednesday.—The Dutch Government, replying on the opinion expressed by Mr. Gladstone as to the attitude which should be assumed by England as regards the Trans- vaal, are about to make an appeal to the fairness of the British nation in favour of the, independence of the territory. Monday, the 10th of January, is named as the date of this embarkation of reinforcements for the Cape. RELEASE OF ME PRISONERS. The Times Durban correspondent says :—The report of the disaster to the 94th Regiment was exaggerated. Thirty men were killed and wounded; the remainder were disarmed and allowed to proceed to Pretoria. The steamer Anglian, with 140 soldiers on board, arrived at Natal yesterday. The Standard Durban correspondent says :—The Boers have released the prisoners belonging to the 94th Regiment, and have sent them to Pretoria. It is supposed that the leaders of the rebellion disapprove of the massacre, and are anxious to diiclaim all responsibility for it. Refugee fami- lies from Utrecht and Standerton, as well as the families accompanying the British columnrhave reached Natal. All telegraphic wires are now cut. The Humber has arrived with troops fro.n England, and the Anglia has also some up with two hundred men. All march immediately for the front. The Governor is leaving with an escort of volunteers. He will go as far as Newcastle, on the frontier of Natal, and will there await the arrival of troops. Telegrams received from Natal on Tuesday state that the Boers have released a considerable number of the men of the 94th, who were supposed to have been slain in the attack. There was hard fighting at Potchefstroom. It is officially announced that the Boers were compelled to re- treat, with the loss of 100 killed and many wounded by the shell fire. In another telegram we are told that the Boers 'attacked the camp on Sunday,but were repulsed with con- siderable loss. The Government are pressing forward rein- forcements and supplies:_ _

div.head: 'RISING IN BASUTOLAND. THREE HUNDRED ' REBELS KILLED.
div.p: THE 'RISING IN BASUTOLAND. THREE HUNDRED ' REBELS KILLED.

The following telegram has been received from the Premier at the Cape, dated Dec. 24th, via Imtata :—Situa- Con in Bdutoland unchanged. Affairs in Caffraria im- proi-ing. Colonel Bakerbad an engagement with Umhlonlo's army. Three hundred rebels killed. Umblonlo wounded; escaped. Umquikely and Nquiliso, the two Pondo chiefs, promise to assist the Government. AFFAIRS IN AFGHANISTAN. - POSITION OF THE AMEER. The Times Calcutta correspondent says :—The latest news from Candahar reports all quiet there. Some raiding has been going .an in Persian Seistan from the Afghan border. The latest news from Herat indicates that the coalition formed against Ayoub Khan has been dissolved, but he is said to be wery•weak there. The telegraph wire has been cut between Thailand Kohat, otherwise the Punjaub border is quiet. The latest Cabul news would seem to indicate that the Ameer is still far from feelitighis position assured. The Koorum Valley has been quiet since the withdrawal of the British troops. -REPORTED MURDER OF DERVISH PASHA. The Daily Chronicle Vienna correspondent says: Accord- ing to a report which has been telegraphed from Scutari, the Turkish commander in Albania, Dervish Pasha, has been murdered. The telegram adds that the crime was committed in consequence of a sentence passed upon him by the Albanian League, where chiefs were assembled at Rakova (?), for the purpose of coniidering his recent conduct. The announcement, however, must. be received with reserve.
, INDIA. A. report that the Biarquis of Ripon intends to resign his post as Viceroy of India is contradicted. SWITZERLAND.'
M. Anderwert, the President-glect •bf the Swisi Con- federation for the coming year, committed suicide on Saturday evening by shootuiglilinself
FRNCE.

A Paris despatch states that there was a terrible explosion of fire-damp on Monday_ afternoon id a pit near St. Etienne. Eleven bodies have been recovered. The-French Senate' on Tuesday, 'adopted the Budget as amended by- the Chamber 'of Deputies. The: Senate had increased certain allowanoes to ecclesiastical dignitaries, but, the Chamber struck out the items of increase, 'and the Senate, has yielded. The session of the Legislature was _ , closed on Tuesday. A serious misfortune has befallen the French ironclad maysrin the lasso! the Richelieu.. The vessel, which was lying at Toulon, took fire on Tuesday night, and smir her moorings. Several of her' crew were injured. The Richelieu ranked in the second class of the French ironclads.' Her armour was 811 inches thick, and she had a central bat- tery armed with 18 and 12 ton. guns. FATRIrITFI,T,L, OOLLIERY EXPLOSION IN FRANCP. . PARIS, December 27.—An explosion of dre-damp took place this afteimodn, in the Lamalolleits, near St. Etienne. Eleven bodies have been recovered I.s to the present; but it is Impossible, as yet, to determine the extent of the disaster. • . The Italian police have arrested two well-dressed foreigners at Milan railiday station just as they were taking tickets for Turin, and the Florence pollee have arrested two 'gentlemen, accompanied by English , ladies, at their hotel. lln the luggage of all these prisoners a quantity' of forged Italian and foreign bonds were found, and the police believe they -have discovered a widely-ramified association , for forging Government bonds. ROUMANIA. Siocks of earthqualse Were felt in Roumania- on Christ- mas-day. The general- 'direction of the disturbances was from nortliTwest to south-met. A rather violent shock was felt at Odessa en Saturday evening. CYPRUS. • ' „ . Recent heavy storms hlve caused' serious' damage in the island of Cyprus.' At Limasol there have been destructive deeds, but notwithstanding this visitation the prospect of the crops is considered very satisfactory. It is stated that eight live' were lost and a large numher .of houses were swept away. - : THE GREEK QUESTION. A St. Petersburg journal states that ,the Russian Govern- ment is in favour of an international, tribunal of arbitration 'on the Greek frontier -questiOn, If it-be accepted by the six Great Towers as well -AO by Turkey and Greece, and the latter promise to accept' the decisions -of. the tribunal. , According to a telegram from, Constantinople the Porte has not arrived at any decision on the Matter. The majority of the Ministers, it is stated, are hr favour of maintaining the offer made by Turkey on the'Srd October, and icrthe event of the Porte accepting the arbitration it will stipulate ~that the-Ottornan troops shall occupy the Balkans. _ The Pert, is ahead to issue a Circular which, while ob- jeciing to arbitra:tien as a means of settling the frontier -question, will propose a new Conference to consider the sub- ject. The news from Athens is of vigorously reneyted military preparation. It is stated that the language of the King on the arbitration scheme was very decidedly negative, even more so than that of his Ministers. At Vienna it is still believed-that the arbitration scheme will be successful. M. Tissot„the French ambassador at Constantinople, has recommended the Porte to accept the arbitration of 'the Powers in the'Greek frontier Question. It is reported from Berlin thahbe Powers have substantially adopted the three conditions stipulated by Germany—via., decision by a majority of four, the expressed readiness of the disputants td abide by it, and the discarding of all 'Coercive measures. Colonel Grivas, a Greek soldier and ,politician, who has been several times Minister of War, has declared to an English correspondent at Athens that wa; with Turkey is an in.

div.head: "EXAMINER,' SATURDAY, JANUARY L
div.p: THE "EXAMINER,' SATURDAY, JANUARY L

1 ItANC+Sililigt ilsT•; yg_ Tllifir' ril'qv! l- BY THE EFi, Rospav GRAD, WELL:— . 1 Lancashire,; :in : the erCrly leths of lie,4reign of Qae i t Elizabetla,-wo sodifferent from the Lan Caahire of to-da , and these differences were so many and . important, that my readers will he interested in a description -of the county ris it waste the :latter half of the 'sixteenth century'. rFe counties have changed more duringethree hundred year. The position of Lancashire, and the general Character of i soil and climate, caused it to be a comparatively backward county, and in the Middle Ages it is but seldom mentioned in history. The word Lancashire does not occur during the Sakon frerlod ; and in Doomsday Book, written about 1089' the part north of the Ribble is ascribed to Yorkshire, and the district between the Ribble and Mersey appears as an ap- panage of Cheshire. The earliest recorded mention of the name Lancashire is to be found in the Exchequer Office. in what is called the Pipe Roll, dated about 1140, the fifth year of the reign of King Stephen. • , At the time -of the Norman Conquest, the population Of England and Wake is computed by Par George Nichols in his History of the -English Poor Law, to have been anent 2,150,000; Lancashire itself was very thinly populated; and Sir Henry Ellis, in Iris introduction to the Doomsday sur- vey, estimates the population rat Lancashire and Cheshire together 'at. 13,000. Doomsday Book, in its description Of the Hundred of Amonnderness, in which Goosnargh--edr martyr's native township—is situated, concludes with these words: "All therm villages and three churches belong to Preston; of these, sixteen have few inhabitants, but how many inhabitants there may be, it is not known; the rest is waste"—a sufficiently suggestive description of the con- dition to which the county had beeh reduced by centuries of conflict, and the recent severe measures. taken by William the Conqueror to break the spirit of the English. Another particular which strikingly illustrates the contrast between the Lancashire of then and now is the value at which landed propesty TM rated. In 1088, when the tax called the , Danegelt was enforced, all the lands between the Mersey and the Ribble were assessed at £129 a year. Even allow- ing for the immensely increased value of money, and reckon- ing the £1 of those days at 110 times its nominal value,the as- sessment only amounted to £13,200; whereas in the year 1841, the aggregate value of land in the same district was £5,525,626; and now, after a lapse of forty years more, dur- ing which the national prosperity has been advancing by leaps and bounds, it is of course very much greater. In the reign of Edward 111., a great change was made in the grevernment of the county, which was then made a Palatinate, in favour of John of Ghent, the fourth son of the King, and so called from having been born at Ghent, in Flanders. Law was to be administered by the officers .and ministers of the Duke, and under his seal; 'and anciently all _ offences were said to be "against his peace, his sword, and dignity," and not, as at present, against "the Queen, her crown, and dignity." In 1343, in the same reign, an inquest was made into the value of movable property in all the boroughs of the kingdom, and the return furnishes us with an interesting account of the progress of the county. Pro- ton, LiVerpool, Lancaster, and Wigan are the only royal bur.9lis mentioned in Lancashire, as Manchester, at this period, did not possess sufficient trade to render it liable to the tax on merchandise and movable property. Preston appears at the head of the list, and was the wealthiest of them all. The document, " Nonarum inquisitiones," states that the ninth part of the goods of men dwelling in the borough of Preston was £6 17s. 4d. This sum, indeed, represents about £lOO in our present coinage ; but what are we to think of the wealth of our ancestors an the middle of the fourteenth century, when the total value of the movable goods of the Prestonians was estimated at little more than £900? ' Liverpool is rated at £6 16s. 7d., Lancaster at £6 13s. 6d., and Wigan at £5 Os. 4d., and it is not unreasonable from this to determine the relative importance of the four towns in the reign of Edward 111, Thus the whole county could boast of "merchandise and movable property," liable to the tax of only £3,500. At the same time, accordineto ' similar Calculation, the town of Norwich possessed pro- perty of this class to the amount of £50,000, and Bristol £30,000. A writer of a previous reign, that of Henri 11., Trevisa, thus describes the speech of the northern counties :—" Some use strange, gibbering, chattering, walling, and grating; then the Nothumbre's tongue (and especially at York) is so sharp, flitting, floyting, and unshape, that we Southrou men may not understand that language." I shall not attempt to determine the comparative merits of the rough honest York- shire dialect, and the broad genial doric of Lancashire, but it was only last Midsummer, at the far-famed College of St. Cuthbert, Ushaw. that it was gravely proposed that an orator from London, who had eloquently discoursed in the purest Cockney accent, should not be allowed to speak again until he had put aside the southern brogue. Of coarse the author of this sapient remark was a Lancashire man; and it would appear that he at least was quite prepared to maintain the cause of our Northern against the Southern speech. If we are to believe Erasmus, who visited England in the reign of Henry VIII., we cannot think highly of the cleanli- ness of the habits of Englishmen in the sixteenth century. According to him the people were generally dirty and slov- enly in their habits, and he attributes to this the virulence of the numerous plagues, with which the country had from time to time been I laded. He describes the floors of the houses as made of "clay, and strewn with 'rashes, under which lay unmolested an ancient collection of beer, grease, fragments, bones, spittle, the deposits of dogs and cats, and everything that is nasty." Miss Strickland (" Queens of England,' vol. 5, p. 424) makes the following statement: PeDornestic cleanliness in the reign of Queen Mary was by no means an English characteristic. When a room was out of order, the floor was neither swept nor washed, Ilut received a fresh strewing of green rushes, just like the littering of a farm-yard, when it is newly spread with straw for the accommodation of the cows or pigs, and the old surface re- maim a festering mass beneath. Thus, layer of rushes accumulated over layer, covering up bones, fragments from the wasteful dining-table, and other abominations. On occasion of dancing all this litter was disturbed by a circle being swept in the midst of the hall; the shine floor was thus clear of encumbrances, while the extra littering was heaped up all round. This custom explains an expression used by Shakespeare and the early dramatists and chroni- clers, of "A hall! A hall !" when persons wished to dance. Such was the call by which_donsesticslauderstoodthey were' to sweep the dancing ring in the hall. How noxious the vapours of the newlrdisturbed compost must have :peen to perioni%warm . withdancing" maybe senriosisd:. -.. . The nobles were not a whit cleaner than the _country gentry; but, as they were usually possessed of several seats, they indulged in the luxury of removing from one to another, when the insects, cherished AI their dirtysustoms, became inconvenient. These progresses they elegantly termed 'going to sweeten.'" That this abominable practice was not unknown to Lan- cashire is idioiriiTuy,--VertnOris discovery made in the year 1856, under the auspices of the Lancashire and Cheshire Historic Society, while makhig.„excavations into what is known as the Castle Ilill,Peewerthans. ' After cutting away some feet df superineumbent earth, they came to what had been a floor, payed, with boulders. On this lay a thick coating' Of black decomposed vegetable matter, resembling a peat bog. 'This had been gradually fornld by successive layers of flags, weeds, hazel twigs, and refuse of various sorts. In some cases the vegetation had been well pre- served. Stems, seeds, and leaves of the common dock were interspersed among the mass, as well as many blackened hazel-nute. A large quantity of bones west found in the rubbish; they. Were generally broken, and belonged prin- cipally to the wild boar, deer, ox, and some smaller animals. Jawbones of the wild hoar were rather, numerous, and some loose tusks were picked up. They appear to have been the refuse of the dinner-table, thrown upon the floor, and after- wards covered gradually with this vegetable substitute for a carpet.

" /few Seasons Marmalade now ready.—Hartley's Mb. jars." On Thursday Mr. R. Knight, the editor of the Statesman newspaper, was committed for trial on a charge of publishing a libel on a nativerdignitary at Hyderabad. . Tim OPENING or Partmeararr.—Mr. Stuart Rendel; member for Montgomeryshire, will move, and Mr. John Slagg, member for Manchester, will second, the Address to the Throne in reply to the Queen's Speech on the opening of Parliament. The Address in the Rouse of Lords.*ll be moved. by Lind Carington and seconded by the tart Of Yarborougho,, FEARFUL Havoc BY FLOODS.—Great havoc was aused by tie floods of Wednesday. At Burnley 14 men who were' at workin a building overhanging the river had a narrow .escape from death. The foundation, of the building was undermined by the violent rush of the water, and the men, warned by the cracking of the walls, had only just reached the door when the outer walls of the workshop fell into the stream. The heavy rain brought down on to the York and Scarborough Railway near Malton part of a cliff which skirts the line, and the first .train on Thursday morning— goods and mail train—ran into the obstruction. The castles and houses of the nobility and gentry were very sumptuous in their way; and, hospitality of the most profuse kind was generally practised by the wealthy barons: but, as has been already observed, the apartments were often in a most filthy condition.

My fair readers will be interested in reading the opinion of John de Brentford of their sex in Lancashire at this time. He says: "The women are most handsome ; their eyes brown, black, hazel, blue, or gray; their noses, if not inclined to acquiline, are mostly of the Grecian form,which gives a most beautiful archness to the countenance—such, indeed, as is not easy to be described. Their fascinating manners have long procured them the name of the Lanca- shire Witches." And Camden, too, was most favourably im- pressed with what he saw in the County Palatine. He writes: "The goodly and fresh complexion of the natives does sufficiently evince the goodness of this county; nay, and the cattle too, if you will, for in the oxen, which have long horns and proportionate bodies, you will find nothing of that perfection wanting that Mago the Carthagenian, in Columella, required." (Quoted in " hardwieke's History of Preston,"p.l44.).

The population of the kingdom had increased but slowly since the Norman Conquest, having little mord than doubled in 600 years. At the time of the expedition of the Spanish Armada, in 1588,.a rough census was taken, and it was com- puted that the inhabitants of England and Wales amounted to 5,000,000 ; but the proportion dwelling in the Northern Counties was far less than it is now. Macaulay tells us that "it appeared in the returns of 1841 that the ancient archiepiscopal province of York contained two-sevenths of the population of England ;" so late as the Revolution of 1689, it was believed to contain only one-seventh, so that all the country north of the Humber and the Dee would amount to little more than 700,000. In Lancashire the number of the inhabitants appears to have increased more than twenty- fold since Elizabeth's time, while in many Southern and Midland Counties it has hardly doubled. Perhaps T shall not be very far from the mark if I put down the population of Lancashire in the early years of the reign of Elizabeth at between 100,000 and 150,000. Of the towns, Preston num- bered but 3,000, Liverpool in 1548, is stated by the Corn- tnissioners for suppressing the chantries as having 4,000 house-lying people, and also a great concourse of strangers by land and sea, so that it might reach from 5,000 to 6,000, and Manchester was not more populous. Indeed Macaulay tells us that, in 1685 more than a century after the acces- sion of Queen Elizabeth, the Kingdon did not possess a Isingle provincial town containing 30,000 inhabitants, and only four numbering as many as 10,000. The country districts were in a very different state of cultivation then from now ; able statisticians have estimated that long after the period of which / am writing, not one- half of the area of the kingdom was under pasture or til- lage; the remainder was believed to be moor, forest, or fen. From books and maps of the seventeenth century, it is plain that routes which now pass through an endless succession of richly cultivated fields then ran through little else than heath, swamp, and warren. We read of districts In which, for a length of forty miles, there was not a single enclosure, and the land on either side of the road is put down as wood, fen march, or heath. Indeed, it seems certain that more than a fourth, part ,q; England has been turned from a wilderness into a garden since Elizabeth ascended the throne. There are many reasons for thinking that Lancashire would be behindhand as compared with the counties nearer to the metropolis, as will be apparent to anyone wile considers its moors and its fells, its mosses and its meres ; and these occu- pied, till a period much nearer-our own, a far larger propor- tion of the surface than they do now. A fair test of its comparative importance with other counties is furnished in a return of a tax in the first year of Elizabeth. The pro- portion of London was about £IB,OOO, the next town in order was Norwich, with its contribution of nearly £6,000, while the whole of Lancashire was not called upon for more than £l,OOO. --- - -

My readers in endeavouring to form an idea of the Lanca- shire of those days must not forget that the great cotton in- dustry had not begun to exist, for not an ounce of the raw material had then been imported into England, though, singularly enough, even in Henry VIII.' reign, Manchester was spoken of in the statute book as a growing emporium for cotton goods; but in reality they were made of woollen and called cotton only because they imitated some coarse fustian goods imported from Spain. In the same reign, Le- land, the king's antiquary, who visited Lancashire about 1540, tells us that coal was worked near Wigan and in divers parts of West Derbyshire. "Mr. Bradshaw had a place at Haigh, a mile or two from Wigan, where he had found much cannel, like sea-coal, in his ground, which was very profit- able to him " (Baffle's Lancashire," 1., p. 194). But the state of the roads confined the frequent use of it to the near neighbourhood of the pits. For a century after the time of which I am writing, the roads of England can be described by no other term than simply execrable. ID 1648, Oliver Cromwell, in his despatch to Parliament, after giving an account of the great battle at Preston, thus describes the road between Preston and Wigan: "We lay that night in a field close by the enemy, being very dirty and weary, having marched twelve miles of such ground as I never rode in all my life, the day being very wet." . Even so late as 1770, Arthur Young refers to the state of the roads between Preston and Wigan In the following in- dignant strain: "I know not in the whole range of language terms sufficiently expressive to describe this infernal high- way. Let me most seriously caution au travellers who may accidentally propose to travel this terrible country to avoid it as they would the devil, for a thousand to one but they break their necks or their limbs -1.,y overthrows or breakings down. They will here meet with rata Which I actually measure& four feet deep, and floating with mad, 'only from a wet summer I What must it be, therefore, in winter ?" And Peter Whittle tells us in his " History of Preston "that, in 1771, "the first stage-coach established in this town was ithcent this time." Sumpter horses were used 'previously to 1 -this in the carriage of parcels and provisions. Strings of pack horses, thirty or forty in a gang, were used for carry- ing coal and lime. The leading horse of a gang carried a bell to give warning to travellers coming in the opposite direction by ay sharp turn or harrow pass. It very fre- quently happened that,the'Roman Causeway between Pres- ton and Wigan -scarcely afforded room to pass, and they were obliged to make room for each other liy plunging into ' the side road, which was sometimes almost kmassible, out , of which they found it difficult to get back upon the cause- way (" History of Preston," 11., p. 61). If I add that, in Elizabeth's reign, there was 'no public post, that a private individual who wished to send a letter 1 to a distant spot had no other means of communicating than AT either a private messenger or a chance traveller; that there was not a single public stage-coach or conveyance plying between Lancashire and the metropolis, but that the Intending wayfarer must proceed slowly and painfully through the miry and uneven roads on foot or on horseback, thinking it matter for high congratulation if he could accomplish thirty miles in a day, and reach his journey's end in ten days or a fortnight, the reader will have some idea of the isolation of the county:from the world at large. There was not a printing press in Lancashire till long after this 'time;' books were extremely scarce; indeed, printing bad been introduced into England barely eighty years. Claughton Rectory happens to be the fortunate possessor of one of the few known . copies of a valuable book printed in 1509 by Wynkyn de Worde, the pupil and successor of Caxton. ..It is entitled " ilLinuale secundum usum Ecclie Thoracen," and is a splendid specimen of the printer's art. The name of the Pope is carefully erased wherever it occurs in the Office, and so the mutilated pages of this work remain a standing monument of the change in the religion of the people made by that ruthless king Henry VIII. _ I will 'conclude by asking my readers to imagine Lancashire before a potato was grown in its soil, before tO-• bacco had been introduced from Virginia, or ii bale of raw cotton had been brought from Asia Minor to Manchester. Yet such was Lancashire in the reign of Elliabeth. -

They were downright glad to tee old Father Christmas and to give him a hearty welcome. He bad to speak to them that afternoon about that fine M o fellow " with jolly face, and beard of greyt with his head all crowned , eleimed especial interest in hire as he with holly. He born on Christmas day, and he was th e (the lecturer) was e first old fellow he ever saw. (Laughter.) They were all in th , e habit of associating Christmas with good cheer. T o a man with a sound digestion, nothing was pleasanter than to stroll through an English town just before Christmas to see the l good things provided to create inward satisfaction. It made one feel like the lad who said " Hey, Mester, I can tell yer what an appetite is; whenever I'm eating I'm happy, and when Pm full I'm tight. • That's an appetite" (Laughter.) What quantities of old English roast beef gaily dressed and decorated graced the shops, suggest-. lug that somebody intended eating a great deal, though it remained by no means certain that everybody would get a Christmas dinner. After relating a laughable anecdote showing how an old gentleman who did not understafid the age of rabbits managed to get young ones from his poulterer, the lecturer went on to say that he supposed none of them ever needed to play their poulterer such a trick, and all they needed to think about was how to cook their goose (a laugh) or whatsoever it might be. And what a splendid affair that cooking was. What a pleasant sound to hear the the pudding singing in the copper, and to have every now and then a savoury odour of the kitchen oven. Men should not be hard upon their wives, who sometimes got a little flushed and out of temper whilst they went about their work. They would be in a nice pickle if they had no mothers, or sisters, or wives to cook their dinners for them. They might go down to the market and make all the pur- chases they chase, and take them home in glee, but woe to them and their households if us woman's hand was ready to prepare the mid-day meal for those she dearly loved. And if she did come wheedling round, trying to get her husband to buy her a new bonnet or dress, and a lot of blue ribbon to tie up her bonny brown hair, he should not grumble, but be a man and buy it if he could. (Laughter.) A young lady friend of his was once reading a paper on woman's worth before a Mutual Improvement Society in Birkenhead. She referred to woman's worth as a cook. A gentleman in criticising the paper in a friendly way, reminded the young lady that the cleverest cook in the world was a man. This turned the laugh against the lady, but it was only for a little while, for rising to reply she said, "Who taught him how to cook; his mother or his wife." (Laughter.) The gentleman gave up the argument, for " If a woman will she will, you may depend on't, And if she won't, she won't, so there's an end (Wt." Speaking of family gatherings, he said those parties were not what they used to be, for sunshine and shadow marked the path mons% had to tread, but still they would not lose pleasure of inviting the circle, though smaller than it Ato be. The family gathering would go,on until a grander union than earth had ever known should be con- summated in Heaven. Whilst great differences existed in different families there was great unanimity of feeling about gathering together at Christmas time. It was an old custom and a good one. The lads, Tom, Dick, and Harry were home for the holidays. What a racket they made to be sure. . The sisters some of them married, and some at service, or in some business, came on Christmas eve and were staying for a week or two, and, of course the little folks were at home as usual. The house was all alive and excitement prevailed. How proud the parents were to have them all there. None at present sleeping under the willows, but all Webs gather round the table in the father's house. Thank God for unbroken and united families and for the possibility of a general gathering at Christmas. None of the old humdrum tunes that took all the life out of them and made them feel as though they were taking part in an execution, but a brisk and lively tune with as-much melody and dance in its tones as possible. Dance did he MY ? Yes, but he did not say they were to do so. Be was speaking of the music, and he offered no opinion as to their nght to spring about like electric automations. Some people said dancing was all right if John took James for his partner and Polly stood with the player. (Laughter.) He did net' know so he could not pretend to say. He knew the practice , had been very much abused, and balls had very much to answer for both •in regard to the physical ill-health, and moral, deterioration of many who had attended them. But' he was speaking of family gatherings, and if 'people must and will romp and play, why they might as well do it artistically as in a heavy and ungraceful way. As to blind man's buff, so far as he WAS aware, nobody ques- tioned that game. It was believed in even by people who were too timid to take part in it. Of course the young men had invited somebody else's sisters. (Laughter.) They all did it is their turn, and their children would do it after them. And now the game was at its height, but, strange to say, young Tom, blindfolded as he was, seemed always to have a tendency to follow Alice---Qoud laughter)-and when he caught her he would not catch anybody else. (Renewed laughter.) They might fall up against him, but he did not want them, not he. His conduct•was most deceptive. There he stood, and ran his hands over her head dress, and then over a chain she wore around her neck, and then round the ring she had on her finger, and at last said, "Why, actually It's Alice," as though he had ever a thought it was anybody else. (Laughter.) Drinking, the lecturer continued, was sadly too common in the presence and company of old Father Christmas, and it would be a splendid thing if they could only change our social customs in regard to that matter. It seemed as though nothing could be rightly done without the drink, add atenth festive seasons as t bristrnas, which they were passing through, infinite mischief was wrought by the un- restrained indulgence which prevailed. In any case he would urge them to Be sober all the while they welcomed Old Father Christmas, and after he had passed away from them as well. And whilst they thus abstained from all evil, resolve that they would do their very best to secure whatever real mirth and merriment was possible as often as Old Father Christmas came, remembering that there still remained very much for them to do before • everybody could be glad and joyous in such ways as he had named. Next Sunday afternoon Mr. Vireatherhead's lecture will be "Once again."

Marshall had told him (witness) that 58. a day would be sufficient when they first begun to use it. Marshall never gave him (witness) any money to pay Hunter with. rie used the storage place for above three months. w il On one occasion h" st out with the horse and cart at Prescot, he stepped on the spokes of the wheel to getPnto the cart when three of the spokes came out. Examined by Mr. Nordon witness admitted that he sizned a paper (the effect of which Mr. Nordon said, was that Mr. Marshall, the defen- dant, pay witness his wages, and ss. a day with which he had to pay Hunter, the plaintiff), but he (witness) was drunk at •the nme.—Mr. Nordon: Did you not spend the money that Marshall gave you to give to Mr. Hunter P—Witness : Mr. Marshall never gave me any money to pay Mr. Nordon for the hire of the cart.—Did you get drunk with the money which had been given you by Mr.' Hunter? No, not for that, but I spent three or four pounds that I received for barrels. I spent it in drink, but Mr. Marshall got it oat of my wages.—Did you do nothing to injure the cart? No; I only put may foot on it to get into the cart.—Mr. Nordon submitted that defendant was not liable for the alleged damage to the cart, and it was:adraitted by the witness Cain that he signed the agreement fof ss. a day.—Ultimately the claim was reduced by :deducting £1 65. Od., the difference between 55. and Os. a week £1 103. for rent of place for stor- ing goods, and 05. 10d. for the alleged, damage te the cart; and his Honour gave judgement for the plaintiff for £7 19s. Od.—Mr. Nordon said that as the defendant had been victimised by "this drunken man," meaning the wit- ness Cain, he sould ask that no costs be given, but' that they , be borne by each side.—His Honour : I think plaintiff ought to have his costs.

CLAIM BY A ST. HELENS WITiELIVItIOITT.-1101ESS Bald- win, wheelwright, brought a claim against Messrs. C. Sayers 6; Co. for £6 6s. 6d. being the balance of account for work done.—Mr. Swift appeared on behalf of the plaintiff, and the defendants did not appear.—lt appeared from the evidence that plaintiff was employed by the defendants to do some work to a gantry, or travelling crane, and on finishing it he sent in his bill which included 30s. for loss of time through the defendants having failed to carry out certain stipulation!, of the agreement.—Some money had been paid on acootmt. —Judgment was given for the plaintiff. A Sr. HELENS GLASS Granntawit's Cram. A young man named Wm. Howard seed James Nuttall and Co., glass bottle manufacturers, for the sum of £6 10s. 7d., for wages, —The plaintiff, who was not represented by any solicitor, appeared to be quite unable to conduct his case, and Mr. Swift volunteered to assist his Honour in arriving at the nature of the claim. It appeared that more than two years ago the firm stopped out of plaintiff's wages 158., as he had spoiled a lot of work in the manufacture of bottles, thus causing the masters great loss. ..Plaintiff, however, continued Ito work up to the present time. In September, 1879, the , earn of 16s. 6d. was stopped out of his wages for absenting himself from work, thus necessitating the employment of journeymen workers in his stead.—Plaintiff said he had nothinglo do with the spoiling of the work as his business was simply to take the hot metal out of the tank at the end of a blow pipe. The damage might have been done by five or six other persons. As to being absent from work he (plaintiff) sent word to the manager to get someone to work for him, as he was troubled with the toothache. The manager, instead of doing this, continued to send round a man who "called" him in the mornings to go to his work. He went to the manager and asked hint why he did so, and the manager replied that he (witness) must go home and stay until he was sent for. He was absent altogether about a fortnight. Examined by Mr. Swift, plaintiff said he did not leave his work be- cause there was a reduction in the price of the willi,—The mother of plaintiff gave evidence to the effect thffher son was afflicted with the toothache.—Mr. Swift said he had a counter-claim against the plaintiff which would overtop the claim made by the plaintiff.—ffis Honour said the father of the plaintiff ought to be the suing party, as he was the man who signed the indenture. On that ground the plaintiff would be nonsuited. It was understood that the costs would not be enforced provided that the defendants were not troubled again. A CALTION TO TRADESMEN—John E. Hayes, provision , dealer, made a claim against Edward Stanley for goods sold and delivered.—Plaintiff said the goods were obtained by Mrs. Stanley.—His Honour: Did her husband know of it ? Plaintiff : I don't know whether he did or not.—His Honour: It is very rash he trust women in that way.—Plaintiff. But she has an income of her own independent of her husband's wioney.—His Honour: But, you see, you have no security in trusting the wife on those terms.—Defendant: My wife never got a ha'porth ef him in her life.—Defendant's wife was then called, and she said she did not owe the plaintiff a copper, and never had anything of him. I bought bread off him and paid for Honour: That's geiting goods off him, is it not ?—Witness: This is my son's debt.—His Honour: Did you go and order these goods yourself?— Witness: I did not.—Plaintiff: She promised to pay for them.—His Honour: But that cannot stake the husband liable, although you have a claim against her morally. She cannot give her husband's authority.—Nonsuited.

, Pants, DE,,c. 27.—M. Laisgant, the deputy. who was mainly instrumental in bringing about the appointment .of the Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry into the conduct of General de. Cissey, communicated to the committee in question, some days ago, a letter from the widow of the late M. Duvergier de Hauranne, the well-known publicist and statesman, accusing M. Emile de Girardin of having.carried on au, ~extensive system of espionage for .the benefit of to'reiga countries, and of hating handed over to Prince Biemarek, through the medium of a female, some important documen4 relating to the organisation of the French Army. The committee having heard the letter read, sent it back to M. Laissant without even retaining' a copy of it. In the_,l Chamber of Deputies, to-day, M. de Girardin alluded to the matter, and said he should have passed over in silent die- dahr the charge brought against him of being the chief of the Prussian spies, had it not emanated from a member of the Chamber of Deputies. He then called upon M. Laissant to retract the accusation. M. Laissant, in reply,. said he had considered ittidsdaty to refer the letter to the Committee of ,Inquiry, and he refused to retract. M: Philippoteaum, the president of the Cissey Committe, stated that that body had declined to make any use of Madame Duvergier's communication. At- the conclusion of the discussion, the Chamber rejected the order of the day pure and simple by 393 votes to 79, and passed an order of the day approving of the conduct of the Committee of in- quiry. ANOTHER TOWN DESTROYED BY FIRE.
THOUSANDS PENNILESS AND HOMELESS. - A MAGAZINE FIRED. • - • •

_ The Line correspondent of the Panama Star and llerald wrote on October 30:—" Iquique was almost totally des- troyed by fire on the 23rd inst., and only the poorest quarter of the town is now standing. A Chilien woman, owner of the Central Hotel, who was in a bad position financially, is said to have set fire to her house; the conflagration spread, and has rendered thousands penniless and homeless." This was followed by a second disaster, which is explained by the ChilianTitnes as follows:—"The magazine of the Morro battery blew up, shaking the city to its foundation. Huge stones were hurled a distance of 500 metres. An artillery sergeant named Marquez was in the magazine under arrest, and it is supposed that he applied .a match to the powder. He and the sentry were killed, and two officers and seven soldiers were wounded, one of the latter seriously. Marquez had only been five minutes in the magazine when the explo- sion occurred. Several horses and mules were killed. At the time 4f the explosion there were in the magazine one quintal and a half of dynamite, two quintals of powder in barrels, and five quintals in bags." EASTERN ROUMELIA.

The" difficulty" with the Governor General of Eastern Roumelia has been arranged. It is stated that Aleko Pasha resigned because the Assembly had from motives of economy refused to sanction the grant of £2,000 for furnishing his official residence. The matter has now been arranged, and Aleko Pasha has withdrawn his resignation. THE PROJECTED REBELLION IN CUBA. We have now the means of estimating the danger from which the promptitude of General Blanco saved the white inhabitants of, Cuba. The exiled " patriots " had entered into a conspiracy with the leaders of the blacks and a re- bellion on an extensive scale waa arranged. Filibustering parties from Dominica, Mexico, aid the United States were to have appeared on the Cnban coasts early in December, but General Blanco, acting with great vigour and with full information, seized hundreds of the leaders in Cuba and sent them on board Spaniah men-of-war. Ti,e promoters of the rebellion intended nothing less than a real war of races, and the gravity of the crisis may be estimated from the fact that the blacks and mulattoes are in an overwhelming majority. The recurrence of disorders in Cuba is unfortunate for Spain at a moment when the colonial forces were being rapidly re- duced, and -an.energetic effort made to ease therburden which the retention of Cuba by force has laid for many years upon the resources of Spain

div.head: AMERICA.
div.p: AMERICA.

• The first dount of the census of the United States, although unfinished, shows already that the population exceeds M,000,000. In 1870 the population was 35,558,271, the increase in the decade being, therefore, no less than 12,441,629. NEST Yonx, Des. 28. Three hundred and twenty thousand immigrants are estimated to have arrived at New York during the present year. CHICAGO, Dec. 28.—There are 14,000,000 bushels of grain stored here at the present time, as compared with 12,000,000 at the same period last year. The officials of the Irish Emigrant Society in New York state that during the three weeks before Christmas they sent 5,000 small drafts to Ireland as gifts from Irish-Americans. In the aggregate these moulded to 5100.000.

div.head: RUSSIA:
div.p: RUSSIA:
A decree has been issued at-gC.-Petersburg, and will come into operation in a few days, by which the import duties on foreign goods are increased. The import duty on salt is lowered,'

The Russian Govdtnment is daily expecting to receive decisive intelligence from General Scobeleff, the leader of the opposition against the Akhal Turcomans, at Geok Tepe, It was announced on Tuesday, that General Karopatkine. who is co-operating with Scobeleff, had arrived within a few miles of the Turcoman stronghold. A Shanghai telegram dated three weeks ago states that the Chinese army in the north was reported to number 200,00 men.

He was still-confinel to bed, and was in a very bad way. Inspector Barnett accordingly asked for a remand.— Anthony Gormley, prosecutor's brother, deposed to being present when the quarrel began, and to seeing the prosecn- tor and the prisoner go out of his house. Ho followed shortly afterwards, and found that his brother had beed knocked elown,and was bleeding and insensible, but he did not see what placed him in that condition.v—lnspector Bar- nett said the prisoners hid only been arrested at two o'clock yesterday morning, and as the prosecutor was unable to pear, and some inquiries were necessary, he asked for a remand.—The prisoners were remanded. -

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 1, 1861.

To-nav we offer our good wishes for the New Year, which has dommenced to the largo circle of our readers under circumstances which we hope and believe they will think entitle us to their friendly appreciation. From this date the price of The Examiner is reduced from three-halfpence to one penny per copy. For a couple of years past we have been endeavouring to make this journal a worthy representative of the provincial newspaper press, on the progressive side of public politics, in the towns and extensive rural district in which it circulates. How far we have succeeded in this effort it is for our neighbours and patrons, rather than for ourselves, to pronounce. We are conscious of some shortcomings. The ideal standard of excellence is seldom reached all at once in any kind of human project. Material and other hindrances intercepting the way to .perfection have to be met and surmounted. But there have been vouchsafed to us many encouraging tokens of public recognition and approbation of our efforts. Neither socially nor politically has our work returned unto us void, or our service_been useless. We have-done some - thing towards awakening local public spirit and rallying the scattered forces of independent Liberalism. Apart from suck results, the poitionof The Examiner, regarded simply as a newspaper, has been strengthen- ing ever since it assumed its existing form. The two infallible signs of growth of a newspaper in the esti- mation of the community have been made manifest in our experience. Our sale has steadily increased; and the advertising department has conspicuously enlarged its bounds, as those amongst us who have announcements to make, for which they require the fullest publicity, have seen the desirability of publish- ing those notifications through ,the medium of our columns. Having this done at least something towards producing a good and useful newspaper for this district, we have been led next to consider whether some further development was not possible and desir- able in the direction of cheapness. If there are numbers who are glad to get the local news of this district for three-halfpence, instead of double that sum, are there not thousands beyond who would regard as a still greater benefit a large paper in which' the same intelligence could be supplied for a penny? This question has for several months now been forced upon our attention more and more by the concurrent representations and suggestions of many friends of The Examiner. Working men with families to support have always—especially at seasons when employment is precarious and wages are down—to give heed to the maxim of Poor Richard, and "take care of the , pence ;" and whilst a good many will indeed pay a larger sum for their weekly local newspaper, rather than be deprived of the luxury, a still greater num- ber hesitate to give more than the penny which has come in our days to be a sort of symbol of purchasable facility. The humbler class of workers want their Penny paper as they have their various commodities and conveniences of other kinds for the single copper I coin. IWe have bestowed serious thought upon this point, and we have arrived at the decision to make The Examiner henceforward a penny paper. The reduction in price will entail a considerable money sacrifice at first start; but we feel entire confidence that the loss will very speedily, perhaps immediately, be recouped by the increased sale. It will answer out own purpose, and that of the interests and principles we advo cote, and that, too, of the business men and public bodies which make use of our advertising columns, far better to secure some thousands more readers by selling this paper for a penny than by con- tinuing to charge the other halfpenny not to get those additional readers. The Examiner, although now reduced 60 per cent, in price, is still very nearly as large a paper as before. It will contain practically the same quantity of reading matter as it did. Its eight large pages of seven columns each constitute it the biggest local weekly penny newspaper to be found in ,these districts of Lancashire and Cheshire, or, indeed, anywhere in the two counties out of' Man- chester and Liverpool. We need not tell our friends that nothing less than a sale of many thousands will suffice to cover the cost of production of a newspaper sheet so large, at the retail price of one penny. Are we too sanguine in expecting that the required extended circulation will promptly be attained P As to quality, our firm intention is not to deteriorate, but to improve, and to go on improving as our mechanical and other arrangements are completed, and as the favour of the community sustains and stimulates our activities. All that is needed in order to render The Ezanitner an abiding and extending power in its dis•

'Me plan agreed upoil by the Board, is one which has proves 'successful In other towns, and there seems no valid reason against its adoption in the government of the local affairs of Widnes. . Mr. Sansom, the new station master, at Widnes, is making it very lively for a number of people who have for sometime 'past been very fairly successful id defrauding the London g • and North-Western Line in that district. The proverb Sdia that every dog has its day, and it is quite evident that the company are determined to put a stop to these irregularities. In this course they are being well supported by the Widnes Bench of magistrates, who have, within the last few weeks, fined several orthe defaulters very heavily. • It is expected that the new church at Halton View, Wid- nes, will be opened in about a month. A Ritranvz or ran VICAR or Holm Tarrarr, ittrw - °Oar, IN Trita AFGHAN Wart.--Speaking of Major Preston, the brother of the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., incumbent •of Holy Trinity, Runcorn, the Broad Arrow says :—Amougst the non-combatants who, as Sir Donald Stewart pointed out, have dons noble service in the field, may be mentioned particularly Surgeon-Major Alexander Preston, 66t1a Regi- ment. This gentleman conducted himself in danger with coolness and a complete disregard for his personal safety. He was wounded very soon after his regiment had begun to take part in the engagement at Kushi-ki-nakud.- He was shot through one arm and both loins and lay in the field helplees till Captain Slade, of the Royal 'Artillery, found him lying on the ground, hoisted him on a gun-limber, and conveyed him into Candahar, and thus gallantly saved a most valuable life. Tin WIDNES WESLEYANS AND THEIR CIRCUIT. FUND. —On Monday, a Christmas tree and sale of work took place at the Lacey-street schoolroom, for the purpose of raising about £7O tor the circuit fund. About two o'clock in the afternoon, Mr. Benjamin Brawn briefly opened the proceed- ings. The tree, which was placed in the centre of the room, was in charge of Mrs. Cooper, Mrs. J. Dnxbury, Mrs. J. Hargreaves, Mrs. Povah, Mrs. S. Robinson, and Mrs. Swale. The articles connected with the sale of work were as various as usual, and were placed upon a stall of which Mrs. Brown, Mrs. Houghton Mrs. Hulme, Mrs. Proctor Mrs. Robinson, Mrs. Joseph Robinson, Mrs. Stringer, and Mrs. Tessyman had charge. The refreshment stall was under the super- intendence of Mrs. Bingant, Mrs. Hartley, Mrs. Lawrenson, Mrs. S. Sadler, Mrs.T. Sadler, Mrs. John Sadler, and Mrs. Seed; Misses. Abbott, Butler, Evans, Jane Sadler, and Mary Jane Sadler. During the evening speaking, singing, and spelling bees were held, which proved very attractive. Taw Runnier BRINE SCHEME.—Great activity prevails in many quarters for the purpose of checking the progress of the scheme for taking brine from Northwich to the neigh- bourhood of Runcorn, to be there manufactured iato salt. At the fortnightly meeting of the Northwich Board of Guardians, on Friday week, Mr. Ward said he wished to Ming forward a motion to the effect that the Board urgently requested the Daresbury Highway Board not to grant per- mission to the promoters of the proposed scheme for taking brine to Runcorn from Northwich, to cross any of the roads or ways under their jurisdiction. He would like to ask the Clerk if the matter could be discussed then, as he thought that day fortnight would be too late to send their request to the Daresbury Highway Board. If it were so, he would move that on that occasion the standing orders be suspended to allow of the passing of the motion.—The Clerk stated that it was quite competent for the Board to take the matter into consideration now. They were allowed to set aside the ' standing orders as to notice of motion on the plea of urgency, and he thought that matter was of great import- ance, as, if the proposed scheme should become an accom- plished fact it would considerably affect the rateability of the district.—Mr. Ward said he believed the question was a very important one. If the scheme was carried out as pro- posed, it would very materially reduce the rateability of the whole of the district. As far as they themselves were con- cerned, he did not think they would be doing justice to those who sent them there if they allowed anything of the kind to take place. They would very soon have a remon- strance front-those outside. As the matter was thoroughly well known to the members of the Board he did not think it necessary to say anything further than that it was to their interest to do all they possibly could to prevent the scheme being carried out. He would therefore beg to move the resolution.—Mr. G. Slater seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—A member said he understood that a great many of the landholders had given their sanction to the pipes running through their property.—Mr. Brunner: No, .o! only one. ) Sr. JOHN THE EVANGELIST, WESTON.—The annum con- gregational tea party in connection with the above mission was.held on Tuesday. Notwithstanding the unfavourable state of the weather, and the fears expressed of a consequent meagre attendance, the promoters were agreeably surprised and rewarded by seeing a larger number of friends than on previous occasions. The mission room this year, thanks to the efforts of some of the congregation, had been suitably decorated for the festival of Christmas. These decorations, which were essentially ecclesiastical, having been supple- mented by others of a more gay and secular character, gave the room an attractive and pleasing appearance. The tea party was followed- by the usual miscellaneous entertain- ment, at which the Vicar presided in MS well-known genial and efficient manner. Of the entertainment itself, which was a marked improvement on previous ones, we may say that the native talent of the village was most ably seconded by Miss Plumb, a young and accomplished pianist and vocalist; Miss Clarke, Miss Grounds, Mr. Yardwood, of Weston Point; and Mr. Ravenscroft, as accompanist. The following ladies and gentlemen kindly gave tables :—Canen Barclay, Mrs. Barclay, Mrs. Bryant, Miss Barclay, Mr. Thos. Balthus, Mrs. Barrow, Mrs. Claudet, Mrs. Ford, Mrs. Light- foot, Poole, Miss Rougier, and Mrs. Vose, Mrs. Adcock, Griffiths, and Morres. On Wednesday evening the children of the day and Sunday schools were regaled with tea and cake. Subsequently the prizes for secular and religious knowledge were distributed by the Rev. J. J. Bryant (curate- in-charge), which distribution was diversified by vocal and instrumental music and recitations. The Drum and Fife Band of the Sons of Temperance contributed much to the evening's pleasure by their enlivening strains. After cheers had been given for the ladies and gentlemen who had pro- vided the necessary f (bids, for those who had given gratui- tous assistance, and for the school master and mistress, a really enjoyable evening came to a close, and the promoters had the satisfaction of knowing that their labours had been more than repaid in the happiness which, at least for ono evening, they had been enabled to afford those who of all can and do enjoy the innocent pleasures of this festive season.

CIMISTMLS DECORATIONS AT R1:12(0011/C PARIAH Clrtritelt.—We have often had occasion to remark upon the propriety and good taste which characterises the decorations put up at Runcorn Parish Church, whether at Christmas- tide or for a harvest festival. This year the great event commemorated was indicated by the text emblazoned on a scroll over the west door, "God sent forth His Son born of a woman," flanked on each side by an Oxford frame, con- taining one of Isaiah's titles, " The mighty God," and 'The Prince of Peace." The union of the Divine and human nature in the person of the Lord was suggested by the words over the north and south doors, " God Incarnate," " Man Divine." At the east end was missed the long text which in former years has appeared under string course on the east wall; but this, since last Christmas, has received a perma- nent decoration, relieving by its warmth of colour the bare- ness of that portion of the sanctuary, and only leaving room for the word " Emmanuel " over the Holy Table, wrought in old English capital letters of holly leaves, tastefully gemmed with holly berries and everlasting flowers. This name is an appropriate sequel to the word which was read on either side of the central light of the east window, " Hark! the Herald Angels singe Glory to the new born King." On the re-table was a floral cross, composed of chrysanthemums, primulas, and other flowers from the con- servatories of Mrs. Charles Hazlehurst, of Halton Grange, Mrs. Wigg, of Halton Lodge, and Mr. Alfred Thomas, of Norton Lodge. The pillars of the nave seemed to have been treated in imitation of a Norman-Gothic interior, when each pillar often exhibits a difference in moulding; so here no two pillars exhibited the same design, several being wreathed with laurel arranged in different ways, another with holly, another with pendant ivy, tic. Our attention was attracted by the pillar nearest the south door, the orna- mentation of which was composed of several species of evergreens, leading, not unnaturally, to the conclusion that it was completed last, when material was growing scarce; but on making enquiries we learnt that the wreathing was composed of the offerings of Sunday scholars in the girls' school, each of whom brought what amount and quantity of evergreen they could procure to be worked up into a "children's pillar." Tho pulpit and prayer desk were ap- propriately treated, the former displaying on each panel an ecclesiastical device in evergreens gemmed with holly berries and flowers; whilst on either side of the chancel arch were the Greek letters Alpha and Omega, each in a suitable frame. Much credit is due to the ladies of the congregation whose lissom fingers achieved so pleasing a result, especially Mesdames Barker, Bryant, Marwood, Meadowcroft, Whit- taker, the Misses Bate, Barclay, Cawley, Crosby, Knowles, Hartley, Mack, Spencer, Statham, Ward, Wiggs, Williams, ctc. The evergreens were kindly supplied by Mr. Robert Daglish, of Aston Hall. Tuere was a fair congregation on the morning of Christmas Day, and a very large one on Sunday evening, when full Cathedral service was rendered with remarkable effect, Mr. B. B. Pierpoint declaiming the recitative, "For behold, darkness," and singing the air," The people that walked," in a style worthy of the reputation he has already achieved as a rising musical artist ; whilst the choir, strengthened by some members of the Madrigal Club, who kindly gave their services, rendered "Unto us a Child is born," and the " Hallelujah Chorus" with a precision and verve (considerably enhanced by Mr. Johnson's skilful accompaniment on the organ) that must have impressed upon every hearer the great truths connected with the Christmas festival,—truthe which the Vicar vividly set forth in an eloquent sermon, taking as his text the single word "Emmanuel. • , PRIMITIVE METHODISM AT ROCK SAVAGE,— OR Christi- mas Day the Primitive Methodists had a very interesting gathering. In the afternoon a Large number of adults sat down to tea, with which the scholars were afterwards , prd- vided. ' Mr. Stokes lent a large room for the public meeting, which was filled with a large congregation. Mr. Stokes presided, and addresses were delivered by Messrs. T. String- fellow, S. Rowland, and the Rev. J. Marton. Several interesting pieces were recited by the children, and a solo was given by Mr. W. Xosworth. A vote of thanks to the chairman for his servicas and kindness in the accommodation which he had provided, brought the proceedings to a close.:, We hear that. the Primitive Methodists are about to erect a school chapel at Rock Savage. Mr. D. Garnett; the presi- dent, occupied the ,chair, but the attendance was not very large owing doubtless to the unfaiourable state of the weather. The following was the programme :—Glee, "Oh! who will &re the downs"; song, "gpur jolly smiths," Mr. Eccles; recitation, Mr. Furness;” pianoforte solo, Miss Nelly Garnett; comic' song, "The Fellah," Mr. Cooper;' song, ".,The merry Zingari, Miss Cavanagh; song, " The • Friar of orders grey," Mr. Warburton; song, "Barney oh Haigh," Miss Newcombe; song, "Firm AS oak," Mr. Eccles; duet, Miss Newcombe and Miss Cavanagh; recitation," The nomination," Mr. Furness; comic song, "Makes a man a. fool," Mr. Cooper ; reeitation, "Billy's rose," Master R. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the,' chairman on We proposition of Mr. Watson, and seconded by Mr. R. Garnett, and the entertainment concluded by the audience singing " God save the Queen." ' THE REPRESENTATION OF WIGAN.—The addresses of the Liberal and Conservative candidates for Wigan were issued on Wednesday night. Mr. Lancaster, the Liberal candidate, in an excellent manifesto, says that Irish grievances are not imaginary, and that purely coercive measures to redress them would be as futile as unjust.. Mr. Lancaster cordially supports the home and foreign policy of the Government. Mr. Powell mainly contents himself with promising to take the earliest opportunity of explaining his views upon questions which occupy the public mind at a time of "more than ordinary critical moment." Mr. Lan- caster arrived at Wigan on Wednesday afternoen,'and was met at the station by a large number of friends, who warmly cheered him, and, notwithstanding a heavy !downpout of rain escorted him to the Hope-street Schools, where he thanked them for his reception, and hoped it was the begin- ning of a glorious victory. In the evening, Mr. Lancaster met the various ward committees of the party.

COLLIRRY MsNsuz,ns' Cnn77:Frosnrs.—The result of the recent examination for colliery managers' certificates, for the North and East Lancashire district, has just been re- ceived. Fifty candidates presented themselves and of these 14 will receive certificates of competency under the Mines Regulation Act. The examiners were Messrs. Waddington, Burnley; Ridyard, Bolton; and Fletcher, Bolton. The fol- lowing are the names of the successful candidate*: —Geo. Elce, 64, Victoria-road, Dakinfield; G. Hollings, Hoyland Silkstone Collieries, Barnsley; Robt. Knowles jun., High Bank, Pendlebury ; Richard Latham, Haydock Collieries, St. Helens; A. B. Blakeley, Hollyroyd House, Dewsbury; Richard Marsh, Heath-street, Golborne, Wigan; Wm. Ash- worth, Crawshawbooth, Rawtenstall ; Henry Barton, Deane, near Bolton; Prank Dorman, The Palace, Maidstone ; T. A. Dickson, 11, Chapel-lane, Preston; .1. H. Johnson, Brayton Domain, Aspatria; L. J. Hall, Furness Vale Colliery, Stock-. port; George Spencer, Harley Colliery, near Shrewsbury; John Pollard, jun., 14,Standlabgate, Wigan. SUDDIN DRATU OF AN OLD Blew, AT ST. HELENS:- Oa Wednesday afternoon,an inquest was held at the Crescent Hotel, Sandfield Crescent, off Liverpool-road, by Mr. Driffield, on the body of Thomas Marsh, who WO band dead in bed on Monday morning. Mary Shattleworth said she lived with her husband at 10, Sandfield Crescent, and de- ceased lodged with her during the last ten months, and was about 77 years of age, and did not work. On Sunday night he was hearty and well, and came into the house at half- • past nine o'clock in the evening. She asked him to warm his feet, and he did so. He got some toast to eat, and went to bed about ten o'clock without making any complaint. He slept by himself in a one-bedded room, and not getting up at one o'clock the following day, William Smith went up- stairs'And knocked at the door, but there was no answer. She went up, turned the bed clothes down, and found deceased with his arm under hie load, apparently having died without a struggle. He was not cold, and was not discoloured at all. He hadriet been in bad health, but she remembered being told a short time ago that he had had a fit,in the kitchen. His breathing was good, and he could walk three miles an hour. William Smith said he had been lodging at the same house as deceased since Christmas Eve, and had only known deceased a few days. The last time witness saw deceased was at seven o'clock, when deceased had something to eat. Deceased had been at a tea party in the afternoon. The Coroner said there was no room for any suspicion as to the cause of his death, and the only verdict could be " Died from natural causes."—The jury returned a verdict that deceased died from natural causes.
