TELE ST. HELENS UNITED 'METHODIST'S ANNUAL CHRISTMAS Tai PARTY.—Un Christmas day the annual tea party took place in the school underneath the chapel in Ormskirk-street, and over 100 persons partook of tea. The following ladies presided over the tables :—Mrs. Weather. head, Mrs. Andrews, Mrs. Higgins, Mrs. Lindon, Mrs. Meadowcroft, Mrs. Chadwick, Mrs Harrison, Miss Owen, Miss Cash, and Miss Scott. The meeting after tea was held in thp chapel, and was presided over by the Rev. H. J. Weatherhead, the minister. Addresses were given by Messrs. Lindon and Andrews. The choir, under the leader- ship of Mr. Duckworth, gave a number of pieces in admirable style, and Miss Wells, with her humorous recitations, elicited loud applause, and provoked hearty laughter from the audience. A vocal duet entitled, i" Very suspicious," was given very effectively, and met with flattering praise. Well executed pianoforte solos were rendered by Miss Aldridge, Miss Esther Forster, and Mr. Thomas Merricroft, and the whole evening was spent most pleasantly, th entertainment extending up to a late hour. ANOTHER DASSENTEE'S FUNERAL AT Lowrox.—The body of a woman named Green was interred on Friday in St. Mary's churchyard, Lowton, which will be rememberfd as the scene of the recent differences respecting the burial of a non-parishioner. Deceased being a Dissenter and a parishioner, advantane was taken of the Burials Act, Mr. W. Hudson, an Independent Methodist preacher at War- rington, conducting the service. The husband of the deceased applied to the Rev. J. W. S. Simpson, v'zar, for the use of bier and pall, and he stated in reply that his church-wardens objected," inasmuch as the law directs no such concession under circumstances of the kind," an 4 with their united decision "of course," he was bound to concur. The husband of the wornaatthereupon applied to the Rev. R. Smith, M.A., rector of St. Luke's parish, church, Lowton, and the rev, gentleman courteously assented, with the significant remark that the consent of his church-wardens for the loan of a bier would be unaecessarv. The coffin had to be carried from the house of the deceased to the churchyard, the distance only being about 150 yards. The words "Cocoa" and " Chocolate" are of Mexican origin. In answer to the magistrate's clerk, the witness said the prisoners were somewhat drunk, but not very drunk. They were very disorderly. Mr. Husband: The last witness says that the prisoners were very disorderly; there was no doubt that they were very drunk. Unfortunately the prisoners were like many other men in Widnes—enthusiastic in spending their money for the purpose of getting tipsy. Whether it is a fact or not that Mr. Sankey refused to give them drink, I cannot say; but it appears pretty clear that they struck the men without provocation. There was one matter to which I think I ought to direct the attention of the Bench, and it is that the assault only took place on Monday, and neither of the men alleged to have been assaulted eeems to have any bruise. I may state that, through me, they express their great regret for what has taken place. It has been insinuated that the case is of a more serioue description than appears upon the face of the evidence. It is remarked that the prisoners threatened to shoot the complainants if they went into Sankey's, but, ' after all, they were not shot, and no guns appear to have been seen. I then submit to the Bench that a charge of drunken- ness will cover the whole affair. , The Chairman: You have not explained what to my mind is the most serious part of the matter, viz, the reason assigned for assaulting these two men. It appears they were 'simply going into a public house to obtain refreshment, on which the prisoners knocked them down, and also accom- panied their voilent conduct by threats that they would do the same or worse, to anyone who went into the house. Now, unless that charge can be met in some way, it very much increases the gravity of their offence. Mr. Husband: I simply suggest that their conduct may have been caused by their havipg been refused drink. The Chairman: Have you any evidence to show that such was the cab? Mr. Husband: No, sir; I merely threw out the suggestions. The Chairman again referred to the serious nature of the threats used, and said the case was not simply one of a drunken man knocking down another. Mr. Husband said the threats used could not possibly have been carried out, as the prisoners had no arms ia their possession with which to shoot. He must leave the casein the hands of their worships. The Chairman: To my mind, the question tor decision is whether this is any concerted action between these men and others to injure Sankey. • Mr. Husband: / think that it cannot possibly be so. The Chairman: If we come to that decision, we shall have to deal very severely with the prisoners. The Inspector said that was all the evidence he was able to produce in the case that day. The magistrates said they would retire to consider their verdict. After an absence ef about eight minutes, they returned into court, and the Chairman said: The Bench have been considering what it is their duty to do in this case. They have every desire to be lenient; but if there be 'any kind of determination on the part of these two prisoners and others to injure this roan Sankey, by intimidating his customers from attending his house, we should have to deal with considerable severity. At present we are not convinced that there is any such concerted action. In the present case, we are displsed to treat it simply as one of assault. If we had taken the other view, that these assaults were part of a conspiracy to injure the man Sankey, the bench would have felt bound to commit the two prisoners for trial at the sessions or assizes, to be dealt with on a more serious charge than that of assault. We have been discussing this, and we have come to the con- clusion that it is not incumbent upon us to send the prisoners for trial for conspiring to injure the man Sankey. However, the assault is a very unprovoked one, and we feel bound to inflict a punishment that will be a warning to the prisoners in future, that in this country men who are going about their business in a quiet and orderly manner cannot be knocked down. The two men in this case were going in a quiet and inoffensive way to get some refreshments in a public house, when you two drunken men met them and knocked them down. That is a kind of proceeding that cannot be tolerated here; and for that assault we send each of you to gaol, with hard labour, for one calendar month, We hope that will be sufficient example to you and to others in the town not to act in this brutal and barbarous manner; but if it be not, and that kind of proceeding con- tinues, and especially if it be found that there is a sort of conspiracy amongst a number to injure this man Sankey, or any other man in the place, by intimidating the people from going to them, the bench will deal with such cases with much greater severity. The police said the other charges would be withdrawn. The prisoners asked that the case might be dealt with by a fine, but the bench said they could nut consent to deal with the case. The prisoners were then removed; and at a later hour were conducted to the railway station, on their way to gaol, by a strong escort of police.

WESLEYAN BAND OP HOPE.—A meeting of the Trinity Wesleyan Band of Hope was held in Victoria Hall, Frod- sham, on Thursdoy evening, when the Rev. .J. M. Bamford presided. A good programme was gime. through very creditably by the juvenile and adult members, consisting of recitations and dialogues, some of which were given with more than ordinary merit. Addreases were delivered by the chairman, Mr. T. Hough, and Mr. R. H. Turner. A collec- tion was made at the close to defray expenses.
Two convicts named Canton and Wilson escaped from the convict prison at Borstal, near Rochester, on Monday. - -

The Liverpool Watch Committee decided on Tuesday to recommend to the next meeting of the Council that the tender of the British Electric Lighting Comppy for light- ing a number of the streets of the city by means of electricity should be accepted. MOODY AND SAMMY : ANOTHER VISIT TO ENGLAND.— Messrs. Moody and Sankey, the American evangelists, have accepted an invitation to revisit Great Britain and Ireland upon a second campaign during 1881. Mr. Moody has just purchased 300 acres of land, and purposes establishing a heme and farm for boys, the sons of parents unable to educate them, with a view to securing missionaries from their ranks.

ANNEAL "PLAT" TEA PASTY' A 2 Sr. Attr.vtqa„— The annual play tea party, in connection with the United Methodist Free Church Schools, was held on Tuesday even- ing, about 200 children assembling for tea at six o'clock. Messrs. Lever and Stott provided the tea and catered in ex- cellent style. After tea indoor games of every description were heartily indulged in by the superintendents, teachers, and scholars. A pleasant evening was spent. ENTESTAHMENT AT WINDLE SCHOOLS, Sr. MUM. —These schools, which serve for day and Sunday teaching, and for holding Church of England service in, and which are supported solely by Colonel Gamble, who also defrays the minister's (Rev. T. B. Maclean) expenses, had the an- nual tea party and entertainment on Thursday evening. Nearly 250 sat down to an excellent tea, the tables being given by the following ladies and gentlemen tables: Mrs. Gamble, Mrs. J. C. Gamble, Mrs. W. Gamble, Miss Sinclair, Mrs. Ansdell, Mrs. W. B. Maclean, Mrs. Thompson, Mrs. Kenwright, Mrs. Halton, Miss Lewis, Miss Henderson (North-road), Mr. Headman. Half tables: Mts. Owen and Mrs. Tyner, Mr. Trotter and Mr. Dean, Miss Hodgett and Mr. Ellison. The entertainment was presided over by Col. Gamble in a genial manner. Several glees were sang by the choir; Mr. Charsley gave several concertina solos, which were well received ; Mr. W. G. Foreman provoked great laughter by singing some humorous songs, and was encored ; Mr. Lindon sang "Pilgrim of love ;" Mr. Howe sang" Nancy Lee" and the "Menagerie;" Mr. Hartley sang, in a nice tenor voice, The anchor's weighed ;" Mr. Bradshaw executed a few solos on the flageolet; Miss E. lienwright and Mr. Atherton gave a pianoforte duet, the latter also manipulating two admirable pianoforte solos Messrs. Howe and Ireson sang " Larboard watch ahoy ;" and Miss Heaton besides accompanying some of the singers on the pianoforte, sang "Jolly blue jacket." Mr. Hy. J. Foreman also acted as accompanist. THE LANCASIIIRE COAL AND IRON TRADES.—III the iron trade there has been only a very limited amount of business doing during the past week owing to the usual un- willingness of buyers to enter into further engagements just at the close of the year. Makers, however, are generally firm, and a moderate amount of business has been done where sellers have had iron to offer up to the end of next June at about present rates. A small quantity of, Lancashire pig iron has been sold over the next three months at about current prices which, for delivery into the Man- chester district, are still quoted at about 465. 6d. for forge and 475. 6d. for foundry qualities, less 2i per cent. Many of the makers in outside districts are now so fully sold that they are practically not offering their iron in this market, and Lincolnshire brands at present seem to be the chief com- petitors; for those delivered into the Manchester district about 465. is being quoted for forge and 475. to 475. 6d. for foundry qualities, less 2i per cent. In the finished iron trade there is no material change, and local bars delivered in the Manchester district are quoted at about £slss. to £6 per ton. The pits in this district have only been working irregularly during the past week in consequence of the holi- days, and there has been only a limited amount of busi- ness doing. House-fire classes of fuel have been in fair de- mand, but common sorts of round coal for iron making and manufacturing purposes have not been much inquired for owing to many of the local works being stopped for stock- taking, Jrc. Slack continues in good demand, and the strike in the Ashton and Oldham districts, together with the anti- cipation of a turn-out of the colliers in other districts at the close of the year, is no doubt tending to increase the pressure for supplies upon holders of this class of fuel, as there is now a considerable consumption of engine fuel for mil purposes going on throughout the cotton manufactur- ing districts. Prices, so far as round coals are concerned, in some cases show rather a want of firmness, and best coal can be bought at under Ps. per ton at the pit mouth, although this is still the general quoted price ; second qualities range, from sts. to 78. 6d.; common house coals 6s. to es. 6d.; with good steam and forge coal averaging about ss. 3d. to ss. ad. per ton at the pit mouth. Engine classes are firm, at about 4s. to 4s. 6d for burgy, and 3s. to 3s. 6d. for good slack at the pit mouth, with common sorts offering at slightly under these figures. There appears to be a general anticipation of ,a stoppage of work in the West Lancashire districts at the end of the month. The contracts with the men then expire in view of the new arrangements under the Em- ployers' Liability Act, and the men may take advantage of I thiain connection with the agitation now going on for an advance of wages,

DISTRIBUTION Op PRIZES AT TIM BRESOOT BOALD Scrtoors.—The half-yearly distribution of prizes to the scholars attending the board schools, through the liberality of W. L. Evans,'Esq., chairman to the Board, took place last Friday. The following ladies aud gentlemen were present during the proceedings ;—Mrs. W. L. Evans, Mrs. Spencely, Mrs. Cross, Miss Hall, W. L. Evans, Esq., Dr. Hall, Mr. Hall, and H. Cross, Esq., clerk to the Board. A good mister of children assembled to receive their presents. In the infants' department, under Miss Macgregor, each child was presented with a bun and an orange, In the boys' de- partment, elegantly bound books were presented for the following heads :—Good attendance, heading the Christmas examination list, and for good ccnduct. The boys, to the number of 190, assembled under the charge of Mr. P. Light- foot, head master, and the assistants, and presented a very clean and orderly appearance. The ladies and gentlemen were received with a salute by the boys on their entrance, and the song, "Evening," (treble and alto) was given with taste and effect. Seventy book prizes were then distributed by Mrs. Evans, after which Mrs. Spencely presented her gift, viz., 18 jackets, to deserving boys. At the conclusion of the distribution, Dr. Hall said he had noticed with great satisfaction the perfect discipline manifested by the boys under their excellent master. It showed that if that was perfect the other parts of instruction would not be wanting. He was glad to notice that the Board schools were in a thriving condition, and he hoped they would continue so. But the best master on earth would have no chance of suc- cess with his scholars unless he was well backed up, and he I was sure that their Chairman was untiring in hie exertions for the good of the schools. He was always ready and will- ing to assist, and it was to be hoped he would long occupy his present position as chairman to the Board. He (the Doctor) begged to move a hearty vote of thanks to Mrs. Spencely and Mr. Evans, for their kindness and liberality. —The boys having heartily given three times three, Mr. Evans thanked all present for the kind reception accorded him. He hoped the boys would continue to work hard at their lessons, so that they would be the more perfect at their work as they grew older. He was glad to notice the atten- dance throughout was increasing in the town, and he hoped such would continue. In their Board schools they had an excellent master and kind assistants, who were always ready to help as much as they could, and to teach them what would benefit them. He hoped the scholars would be attentive to their studies, and give as little trouble as pos- sible. Of course, boys would be boys but he (the chairman) wanted them to play as hard as they liked when in the yard and on the swings, but when in school to work just as hard.

Their conduct and language showed that treason and conspiracy lay at the root of the matter, and the ultimate aim was, as one of the defendants had elegantly put it—"to free Ireland from the vilest Government that ever cursed the earth." The object of Her Majesty's Government in instituting this prosecution was not to restrict liberty of speech, but rather to deliver the country from an intolerable tyranny by which the individual freedom was overruled. The Attorney General had not con- cluded his address when the Court adjourned. • In the prosecution of the Land Leagures at Dublin the whole of Thursday's sitting in the Court of Queen's Bench was occupied with a continuation of the Attorney General's opening speech. The learned gentleman cited passages which occurred in speeches made by the traversers in different parts of the country, wherein doctrines at variance with the law were openly taught. Chief among these were the doctrine that all rent waste be withheld, or only so much given to the landlord as the tenant, after maintaining his family and paying other lawful debts, could afford. The landlords were publicly denounced as 'thieves and mur- derers." It was obvious, the Attorney General said, that the , natural consequence of this teaching, pursued persistently for months, must be to produce feelings aef hatred amongst ! the mass of the people towards the present owners of land in ' Ireland. To go about preaching this kind of sedition could not be tolerated in any country pretending to be civilized , and a joint.stock company got up for the purpose of doing it was an illegal and mischievous conspiracy. The Court again adjourned, the Attorney General not having concluded his address.

LAW AND ITS COSTS. Sir,—The present expensive legal mode of procedure is sightly engaging public attention, and probably, would all who have been engated or dragged into law suits come for- ward aad relate publicly how they have fared at the hands of the gentlemen of the." long robe," we should have a whole- some =peal of the law, and that admirable society, '"The Incorporate Law Society," would probably do greater ser- vice to the public in stepping in oftener, and thinning the ranks of the proverbial " slow-to-heaven-walkers." The season of this backwardness on the part of solicitors' clients is not far to seek, for it is natural that the successful client is net desirous of having his success curtailed by publicly admitting, his pecuniary losses in his accomplished achieve- ment. whilst the defeated candidates are naturally still more desirous of keeping their defeats hidden from public gaze and irony. Natural as this feeling is in all of us, it cannot be denied that it is purely "false shame," which is the cause of this a•neralment. In view of the incalculable mischief which these suppressed facts not only do to the suffering solieitors' clients, but also to society at large, by partly act- ing as an ificentive to lawyers of pill* en the agony—who kn'ow very well that their dupes long for nothing more than abiaien, gaspless retreat,"—it may be further contended that from a Christian point of view we owe it to all our fellow-men to show that amount of charity which we our- selvee would expect from them if they possessed certain knowledge profitable to ourselves. Consider:diens such as these impel me to the publication Of the following fact, which relates to a case in which, after allowing a certain party a two years' outstanding account, in the hope that he would pay me without having to go to law, I still found myself compelled to have recourse to "legal measures." I won the day, obtained £3 in addition to the full amount of the elaime (f.. 40 58.), and my defendant was also ordered to pay my costs ot the cause and of the reference, and to bear kis own ones; in this manner I obtained the most favourabld 'verdict possible! So far so good, but now to the "profit and loss account :" Cr. a ad,

a ø.d. Asenmt payment to 'Payment to lawyers myself by my law- for contest ot trial 28 0 0 yers ............... 50 0 • Attendance at court -. 30 • Apparent balance in Claim for debt ra- iny favour ............ 2 1 5 S lowed .. ---'suPposed balance in ATI 5 0 my favour en 5 • Fancy my surprise when after having had the balance held cut to me for several months my lawyers inform one that owing to the heavy charges of their Manchester agents the balance, instead of being in my favour, would be £45 12s. Od. against me. This charge thus makes a difference of £66 Vs. 3d. to me, or I am called upon, after receiving the most favourable verdict attainable, to lose not only the full amount of the debt, but £26 12s. 3d. besides' to say nothing I of the time and money lost in attending my lawyers, and in travelling to and fro. That I engaged se-esteemed respec- table lawyers no one will doubt, when I tell them that I at Altrincham were my solicitors, and that they on their part employed— of Manchester' to act as their agests proves thA an equally respectable firm was concerned. A Mr more important question involved in this matter, as far as the general public is concerned, is that if legal firms of accepted respectability treat their confiding clients in this way, what mat' be expected from the "rag, tag, and bobtail" et the honourable profession? Let your readers take these facts at their value and I will only add that my solicitors obtained £ll4 value, 4d. front the defendant to this F4-tion; that their agents' bill to them (inclusive of legal smart expenses) was £5O 4s. 21. (or may be less), whilst their bill tome reached the imposing figure of £l4O 18s. 7d., find all these magnificent pocket-fillings for the recovery of if comparatively paltry £4O! Qui, custodiet ipsos custodiet? Who shall guard the guards themselves 7—Yours truly, A. TOLUAUSEN, jun., C.E. Partingten, 23rd December, 1880.

A NEW PEACE AND ARBITRATION ASSOCIA'.I. A. WARNING. Slx,-1117111 you kindly permit me, through the medium oi your columns, to offer a word of caution to the friends of " Peace against being misled by the circulars of the New Peace and Arbitration Association, %thick are now being sent round for adherents and subscriptions. These circulairs are .oent out by a Mr. Lewis Appleton, who formerly belonged to the original Peace Society, but who, for very good reasons, was requested by the committee to terminate his connection with it. One of these circulars was received by Mr. Thomas • Eirchall, one of our vice-presidents, who, seeing that the objects and principles which it set forth were precisely the same as those of the old Society, was under the impression . gist it came from the central office, As many are liable to ilhe same misapprehension, I think it needful to explain that it has no connection whatever with the Peace Society of which Mr. Henry Richard, M.P., has been for so many years Idle leader, or is it connected with the International Arbitra- tion Association, of which we have a branch in Warrington. Wile following is a letter which I have received from Mr. • Menry Richard M.P., upon the subject : •• Cardiff Dzeember IT, MO.—Dear Sir,—l am very sorry that c--Ir. Birchall kas been misled, in reference to the Arbitration and Peace Association. I think that as such mistakes are not only likely but almost sure to take place, the promoters of that organisation ought in justice and honour to state that they ate' Sot connected with the older society, and all the more are they bound to do so, as Mr. Appleton was formerly in cur service. Sind unless he says the reverse, would naturally be considered as still sustaining the same relation to us. I need not tell you Vast it is not in any way with our cognizance or consent, but very much against our wishes that this new movement has been started. They don't profess, so far as I know, to do anything, abet we are not doing already, and it seems to us that there is so room. and no necessity for a second society, and can have no ether effect than to divide the Interests and resources of the ' friends of pelce. I hope you will :make this kaovrn as widely as pmeible amongst the supporters of tke Peace cause at War- renton and its neighbourhood."—Yours truly, HENRY RICHARD. By inserting this in your next issue you will greatly oblige,—Yours faithfully, A. RA:THRONE, Hon. Sec. radjate, December 22, 1830.

THE WESTON SALE OF WORK. Sir,—With reference to "Iconoclast's" rather severe criticisms on my attempt to give justice to the parties con. werned with the "wax-work "affair at the Weston sale of work, I beg to say! consider the letter as a clever attempt to hide az! untruth. The question is, had the gentlemen nahaed in lie former part of my first letter anything to do with the affair or cot? I say not. "Ic4noclast " says one of the gentlemen had. What part he took in the affair I don't know. Certainly one of the quartet did come to the last practice, but he did not take any active part in the matter whatever, not even demur at the style of any of the model's dresses. By the words "the idea originated," I simply meant I{A^srs. Harrison and Norman were the originators, dm., u-Ait the thing in Runcorn; knowing perfectly well that it had been very successful in many other places. With regard to • 'lconoclast's" attack on my youth, I will refer him to Pttes reply to Walpole on the subject, which will, no doubt, answer him better than I can. "Iconoclast's" letter is certainly a triumph of literary art, and to all appearance he has the upper hand of me, being such a clever man at con.: koversy and at everything else except mind \ng his own business, which habit he does not seem to have cultivated. --"With regard to the " Jericho " phrase, I presume " Immo- ‘!.. *last" has obtained this oat of an almost extinct edition of Shakespeare (a copy of which he retains as an heirloom), 815 I have never met with it yet. Certainly "Iconoclast" will reply te this, or his nature would deny itself; but as certainly I shall take no further notice of it, but leave my antion to the generosity of the public. Although " Tabitha Singrileton " for the time being, I beg to subscribe myself snider another title, which is JUSTITIA. Runcorn, December 29, 1880.

-- The weekly, meeting was held in the Boaribroem, at the Workhouse, On Wedaesday. Present—Mr. W. Darbyshire (chairman), the lie. G. F. Roberts, Bev. J. Yonge, Messrs. Cooper, Woolfall, Kilshall, Owen, Cartwright, Garnett, Blackhurst, Wallington, Bowden, Longshaw, Brown, Loughlin, Pennington, Gibson, Balharry, Houghton, Win- stanley, Humphries Swinton, Harrison, Appleton, Hall, Barber, Fairhurst, and J. C. Sutton (clerk). . THE STATE OF THE HOME. The MASTER (Mr. Mackey) reported that there were 493 inmates in the house, as against 508 in the corresponding week in last year. Of 170 vagrants relieved during the week, 148 were men, 18 women, and 4 children. There were 4 cases of scabies, and 3of whooping cough. . PRESENTS TO THE CHILDREN. The Msannes journal also contained an entry that on be- half of the sick children and little ones, Mrs. Mackey would like to thank Mr. Buck, of Sankey-street, for a box of Christ- mas cards he sent for them; and also Mr. Robert Heaton, for a box of oranges. The latter gentleman also wanted to send a couple of barrels of beer for the old people's dinner on Christmas day, as did Mr. William Bolton, of Mersey- street. He replied te both gentlemen that as the Board had decided there was to be no beer at dinner on Christmas day, he must respectfully decline to accept their generosity. THE COST OF THE MEDICAL OFFICERS' RETORTS." BOY- FATTING " DR. SPINES. The minutes of the Barracks Committee stated : A report of the superintendent was read to the effect that the children had enjoyed a very happy Christmas. They were bountifully supplied with roast beef and plum pudding, and were entertained with music, songs, dances, recitations, &c. On behalf of the children, Mr. Mines, thanked Mr. Lythgoe, confeitoner, for a liberal present of sweets. It was resolved that a gratuity of five guineas such be recom- mended to be allowed to Messrs. Gornall, Joseph, Watkins, and Sephton, for their professional assistance in the matter of the enquiry into the condition of the barracks. Mr. BLACICIIIIRST, in moving the adoption of the minutes, drew attention to the allowance of 20 guineas to the four gentlemen who inspected the barracks at the time Dr. Spinks inade a charge about the place being unfit for the children. He thought 20 guineas was a very large suns of money for the services rendered, and he said so the previous day at the meeting of the committee. However, it was allowed to pass by the majority of the committee; but he I should not like the amount to be passed by the Board with- out the members knowing what they were passing. He left it to the Board if they were willing to pay so large a Mtn of money for so little services. Mr. HARRISON said that in order to enable the Board to judge as to whether the amount was reasonable or not, he should be glad if Mr. Blackhurst or any other gentleman would give them an idea as to what the services were. Major CARTWRIGHT: I would beg most respectfully to ask has an application been made by these gentlemen to the committee for a gratuity? The CHAIRMAN: I think not. Mr. BLecicuunsT: I think it was the gratuity offered. Mr. WALLINGTON seconded the adoption of the minutes. He said from information the committee received on Tues- day from those medical gentlemen it occupied a great deal of their time in going round the barracks and the house to make an inspection. Some of the gentlemen, he believed, visited the place two or three times—[Mr. Winstanley : Three timesl—and there had been an7application—perhaps not a formal one—for a gratuity for their services. He understood the money could not be allowed in any other way than as a gratuity, and if the Board remembered what it had cost those gentlemen to obtain their reputations [Mr. Blackhurst : Nonsense !} five guineas was not too much to give them for their services. Major Canna-num: Wonderfully liberal with the public purse ! Mr. Wartmoroto said that amount was allowed by the committee in consideration of the services rendered. The committee considered they were entitled to the allowance. • Rey. S. YONG!' said he was present at the meeting of flka Barracks Committee when this matter was brought forwafd by Mr. Sutton. He said a representation had been made to him of some kind or other by some of these medical men to the effect that they had stated when asked if the reports were not part of the contract with the Board, that it was an extra duty, and in consideration of that fact they thought the Board ought to allow- them a fee, or gratuity, or what- ever they chose to call it, for the services they had rendered in the matter. It appeared to him if that representation was correct the Board had only one course to follow. They could not expect the medical Men to come .from Newton for nothing. If the Board resolved apon a certain course, the Board as an losesourable body ought to pay the medical men for carrying if out, and on that principle he seconded the adoption of the motion which appeared on the minutes of the Barracks Committee. If the Board looked at the matter in that light they would not pooh pooh it in the way Major Cartwright seemed to do—(laughter) ; and he could only say if the BoNrd did not see their way to pay these medical men Major Cartwright ought to do so, as he and Dr. Spinks certainly got up this " mare's nest " about the unhealthiness of the barracks. (Hear,bear, and laughter.) Major CARTWRIGHT said they had the reports from the medical officers and they had also a report from Dr. Mouat that was published—but the public bad not even the benefit of it—in pamphlet form by the clerk, together with the doctors' reports on the condition of the barracks and the house. .They spent the public money, and he thought the public ought to have had the benefit of that report. Now it never:was published. Why? Simply because the Clerk did not read it over. The CHAIRMAN : I think we are wandering from the subject. Major CARTWRIGHT: Oh, no; we are not. Has he not charged me with being the cause of this? I am speaking to the point, sir. Now he charges Dr. Spinks and me with this. I fail to see it. It may be my friend Mr. Yonge tried to be witty and to make a hit, hut it was a very weak one in my opioion—(laughter)—because here is Dr. Spinks, the very one I suppose you proposed to give 5 guineas to yester- day. ("No, no.") Then you leave him out in the cold? Are you going to "Boycott "him? (Laughter, and "Yes.") Oh ! that is it. You are going to keep the doctor out in the cold, are you? You are going to "Boycott" the doctor, are you? I think that is not fair. His report eras very similar to Dr. Mouat's. Of the reports of the medical officers in this union, Dr. Spinks's was the best in the lot. I should suggest, if you do come to the conclusion to.give these gentlemen that gratuity—although Mr. Yonge thought I was going to oppose it, I armnot—if you think it proper to give them 5 guineas each, don't leave out your medical officer in the cold but serve all alike, and I am per- fectly satisfied. The CHAIRMAN : Dr. Spinks, as medical officer of the , barracks, has already had a gratuity for his services. Major Carrsvoinwr : He has not had a gratuity for his report. Mr. Yonge said it was extra work. Rev. J. YONGE was very sorry Major Cartwright was so obtuse. He thought he was chaffing the Board, because he was aware these, gentlemen had no connection with the barracks whatever.. They. were called in to do special work, and to give a special report. Dr. Spinks was the medical officer of the barracks. , Mr. Wrlss-matLET said if Dr. Spinks had been "Boycot- ted," he had been "Boycotted "in a very pleasant manner, because they had given him £3O for his services at the barracks, and seeing that all the work had been taken away' from there to the barracks, the Board had treated him handsomelytand neither Dr. Spinks nor any of his friends had reason to complain. Mr. HARRISON certainly supported the committee, as the ' committee were better acquainted with what those gentle- men were entitled to than the Board. Mr. GARNETT sympathised with what Mr. Blackhurst had said. It was simply a question of amount, and he thought the amount was too much. (Hear, hear). HI belief was, if the matter was inquired into, some of the medical men did not make more than one journey, which, if made to some wealthy patient, would be covered by a very much smaller sum of money than they made by special reports, which had been paid for in too liberal a way. (Hear, hear.) Mr. BLACEITURST : That is my opinion. The CHAIRMAN : I should like to say that I thought this amount too much. The sum which has struck me as being sufficient is £3 3s. for the two country doctor s, and £2 2s. for the two town doctors, as the country doctors had to come a longer distance than the town doctors. Mr. HARRISON I think there ought to be a distinction certainly. Mr. WINSTA.NLEY believed if the Board :offerreci the medical officers less than £5 ss. Od. there was a very strong probability of its being sent back. Major CARTWRIGHT : I should not like to trust them. It would he like getting butter out of a dog's throat. Mr. OWEN having supported the minutes, Mr. HALL proposed as an amendment that the medical officers out of town be paid £3 3s. Od., and the town doctors £22s. OA. each. Mr. BOWDEN' seconded the amendment which:was carried only five gentlemen voting against it. With this exception the minutes were passed. THE COLLECTION OF PAID RELIEF. The Crtaiumax moved that Messrs. Harbourne and Gar- nett be appointed collectors of paid relief for their respective districts, and that they be paid a commission of 10 per cent. upon the rabies recovered- by theta': " ' Mr. Hammon seconded the motion as he could not help. thinking it Isbuld be both a god and 'economical arrange- ment. It left the newly appointed officer at liberty to devote himself exclu.sively to the duty, the Board [might assign to I him to perform. Mr. WINSTANLEY believed they would do wrong by ap- pointing relieving officers who had already too much to do. The Union lost money Issr the officers not being able to, thoroughly investigate the relief cases. Mr. Haim moved an amendment that the new officer should have the appointment of collector. Mr. BLACEIIIIRST seconded this, and after some discnssion the amendment was carried by a majority of 11 vete& CANVASSING BY CANDIDATES. • Rev. J. Yeretak, referring to the advertisement for an assistant relieving officer, Ac., said at the foot of the adver- tisement they were told that canvassing the Guardians IVO strictly prohibited. That was in consequence of a resoln- tion passed by the Board, upon the motion of Mr. Harrison, seconded by himself, some months ago. That resolution had been violated in every respect in this particular case. He called attention to the matter for the reason that when the Saari prohibited a thing steps should be taken to en- force the prohibition. But One of the candidates said, from the Premises which bad been given to him by members of the Board, he was certain to secure the appointment. That was very unjust to the other candidates, and he thought the members, of the Board should refuse point blank to give Promises of support.

A RUNCORN AITSTERY, On Christmas morning, as Thomas Houghton, a night watchman at Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele's works, Old Quay, Runcorn, was walking along the side of the Old Quay Marsh, he observed the trunk of the body of a female. He gave information to the police, and Inspector Hollingworth and Sergeant Morris went to the place. After securing the trunk, which had no arms, they saw the bead floating near, and brought it to the side of the stream. The remains were then placed in a sack, and taken to the Egerton Arms Hotel. The chest was found to be covered with a bodice of mauve- coloured stuff; underneath this was part of a red flannel vest, and tied round the body was a portion of a calico skirt. The legs were covered with black merino stockings, and fastened with leather straps. The age of deceased was be- tween 30 and 40 years, and death is supposed to have resulted from drowning. Very little light was thrown upon the matter at the inquest, which was held by Mr. .Ridgway, on Monday last, at the same hotel. The coroner again referred to the imperative necessity existing for a mor- tuary in Runcorn. Mr. James Percival acted as foreman of the jury. The tirst witness was Thomas Houghton, who said he was a night watchman at Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele's works. On Saturday morning, about nine o'clock, he was walking along the side of Old Quay Marsh, when he saw the body of deceased lying on the bank of the river. On ex- amining it, he found that it was quite nude, with the excep- tion of having en a pair of stockings fastened with garters, and a portion of a dress. He went to the police office about the matter. _ _

Sergeant Walley said that from infcrination received from the last witness he went with him to the Old Quay Marsh, and found the body there, The head and part of each arm were gone. On a further examination, he found the head near the edge of the water. He obtained a bag, and took the body to the Egerton Arms Hotel. Dr. McDougall deposed that he had examined the body of deceased, which was that of a female who would be about five feet high when alive. The head was separated from , the body, and partially covered with black hair. The twit:. ' front teeth bathe lower jaw were goat, but he fonnd them in the mouth. The third tooth in the upper jaw was also mis- sing, and the tongue was swollen and protruded somewhat. The eyes were out, and the greater portion of the chest and abdomen was gone. The arms were off at the elbows, and the upper part of them were denuded of flesh. The chest part of the trunk was covered with a bodice of a mauve coloured stuff, buttoned in the front, and underneath it was 'part of a red flannel vest. A portion of a calico skirt was tied around the middle of the body. The legs were covered with black merino stockings, fastened with leather straps. The body must have been in the water a considerable time, and it was impossible to state accurately what had been tile cause of death. He, however, leaned to the belief that death occurred through drowning. The age of deceased would be about 30 or 40 years. In removing the stocking from the right leg, he noticed a quantity of sand mixed with coal dust. The Coroner asked the witness if he could form any opinion as to the position in life which deceased had occu- pied. Dr. McDougall said it would be impossible to do so, as the features were gone, and the body was more like a mummy than anything else. In answer to another question, witness said he was of opinion that the head found belonged to the body . The Coroner said this was all the evidence to be brought before the jury, and he recommended them to return a ver- , diet of "Found dead." The jury accordingly followed this course. • The Coroner remarked that he did not know whether it would any • good for him to again refer,to the necessity which existed in Runcorn for a mortuary. He had fre- quently spoken upon the question on previous occasions-- and was sure that every juryman would say that it was not fit for a corpse like that which they had viewed to be at anybody's house from Saturday until 'Monday. He could only say that he wished the jury in that case—although•he respected every jury, however composed—had been' consti- tuted of members of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, as they would have seen something which would hate led them to take some action in regard to a mortuary. They would remember that at one of the last inquests which his .40puty attended several publicans had refused to take in the body, and he-ahould not have been at all surprised if the landlady of that house had-refused to take in the deceased. He did not think that any amount of money=andle had no power to allow a large sum—could recompense anyone for having a corpse like that in the house. He had been asked whether he would give his opinion as to where a mortuary should be erected, but this: did not matter to him. :lie wchald hold the inquest in the street if, it were so wished, but he certainly did think it a surprising thing that in a town like Runcorn there was no mortetary. , The proceedings then terminated: ' , A steamer, believed to be the Montgomeryshire, which - sailed from London a few days ago for China, has been lost en the Spanish coast. The crew, numbering, at least 50 `hands, were all drowned. The Montgom.eryshire was on her Bast voyage. The CHAIRMAN: That means not until Mr. Darlington' comes to audit in tbe usual course. . 'The CLERK: That is so. • , The CHAIRMAN: When will ha come? The CLERR: In three months abont. About the 25th of April: • ' ' Mr. JACKSON, who had, during this conversation been Standing, asked that he might be allowed to make an explanation: Jonadab Prescott's hense furniture, they would be aware, had been taken Possession of by the Guarantee Society-, and they would also be aware that Prescott had been doing the work of two relieving officers for 14 weeks, and from what he had been told by- their Chairman be was entitled to 14 weeks' pay at the rate of £lOO per annum, consequently Prescott would want £27. There was also a month's salary of 8/. 6s. Bd. due to him, and if 'they did not advance him that Mr. Prescott and his family would become chargeable to the Union. H Jackson) was prepared to give the Board a cheque for L(MB (Mr. 81., provided that a month's salary be paid to Mt Prescott. He would give a cheque that day and they could hold it over until things were straight. He thought, cod- sidering the harsh treatment,Mr. Prescott had reed:red— Voices : No, no, (and sensation) and calls of "Ordei." FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds, Councillor Monks, and Ziba Armitage, Esq. Dnrrtm, &c.—Martin Lully, drunk in Scotland-road, on the 18th ult.—He was fined in the costs only.—John Smith, and Doctor Dickenson were each bound over to keep the peace for fighting on the A sed premises of Harriet I Stringer, the Chesapeke Inn, ns-end, on the 18th inst. _Martin Hardy, for fighting in N inwick-street, on the 18th ult., was ordered to find recognizances to keep the peace.— W. Branch, drunk in Allen-street, on the 18th December, was fined ss. and costs.—Catherine Quinn was charged with assaulting Mary Quinn, on the 18th December. She was bound over to keep the peace. . PLAYFUL Yourns. —W. Hopwood, Jno. Flynn, and Michael Melior, three lads, were each charged with com- mitting wilful damage to a window the property of Thomas Ury, on the 19th December, doing damage to the amount of ,9d. "Being Christmas time," the lads were let off on pay- ment of 23.10 d. each. MONDAY.—Before Major Cartwright, Alderman Burgess, ' Councillor Fairclough, and Mr. Z. Armitage. INEBRIATES.—James Bennett, charged with being drunk in Sankey-street, on Saturday night, was fined ss, and costs. —William Parr, drunk in the Market-place, on Saturday, was fined ss. and costs.—Margaret Fleming, an old offender, ,drunk in Bridge-street, on Saturday, was sent to prison for fourteen days.—James Bennett and James Scully, drunk in Sankey-street, on Saturday night, were each fined 55. and costs. ALLEGED AOGRANATRD ASSAULT.—ThORISS ALUIDieII WAS charged with being drunk on School Brio, early on'Sunday morning, and also with committing an aggravated assault an Annie Spencer.—Mr. Moore appeared for the defence.— The charge of drunkenness having been proved by the police, the complainant said she was coming home from her mother's house when the prisoner came behind her and assaulted her. She cried for her husband, and the prisoner ran away.—Pr. Moore said the defendant had simply de- fended Mrs. Spencer when her husband was beating her.— William Phcenix said he saw the complainant on School Brow being beaten by her 'husband. They were both drunk at the time. The defendant tried to separte them. Her husband then went &wily, and he (witness) also went away. —William Jackson gave corroborative evidence.—The case was adjourned for the attendance of complainant's husband, bail sbsesi yri Lg To allowed. 1, ALANDLORD AND A CONSTAR/a—Michael Loftus was charged with being drunk on Saturday night in Buttermarket-street.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and also admitted having assaulted John Jenks, the landlord of the Fox Inn, and P.C. Monaghan on the same occasion.—Fined 20s. and costs. , REFUSING TO QUIT.—John Marshall, a bad character, Ida sent to prison for three months on a charge of being drunk in the Crown and Sceptre yard on Sunday night, and with assaulting John Lake and refusing to quit the public- house. _ _

On being charged the prisoner said "Is that all you have got against me." On the application of the Chief Constable, the prisoner was remanded until Friday, to enable further en- quiries to be made.—Mr. Rigby said he thought shopkeepers very much: to be reprimanded for exposing goods near a public-house in the streets. They offered a' great tempta- tion to people who were very thinly clad &c. to help them- selves. He should advise 3ir. Waring, and the Bench would advise him, to be more circumspect in what he put eut. He felt it very much that persons who were not more honest than they should be, should have temptations thrown In their ways ." Ceram use xma Acr."—Jarnes McCormick was charged with stealing 21b. 7oz. of roll tobacco, the propertk of James Atkinson, King-street.—On Monday the prisoner went into the shop, and was about to leave when he was observed and detained. When charged with the offence at the police office, the prisoner said, "I went into the shop for the pur- pose of stealing, but was caught in the act."—The prisoner was committed for one month's hard labour. INTERRUPTING CHRISTMAS FESTTVITHts.—Sohn Hennessy, Michael Hennessy (brothers), and Kate O'Brien well-known characters, were charged on warrant with having assaulted / and beaten Peter Garland, early on Saturday morning, the 25th December.—The prisoners and prosecutor all lived on Cropper's Brew, Buttermarket-street. On Friday night the prosecutor and several friends were having a glass together, and enjoying themselves, when the prisoners with 'others burst open the door. John Hennessy and Kate O'Brien ifeTht he r e prisoners herself broke him knocked prosecutor on the floor, " caught " his head, and b hirmisvoenryba.kdilcyk.Hiserw. abused ede p ers ea h the squares in the window, broke open a let of drawers, pitched a burning lamp across the room, and "smashed everything in the house." Michael Hennessy also threw a bottle through a bedroom window where two chittlren were lying , Besides prosecutor and his wifg, two witnesses who gave.] evidence were also kicked by the prisoners.—The prisoners were each fined 20s. and costs, or in default one month's im- prisonment. The prisoner Michael said he would not give_ them "a red halfpenny," and the prisoners were removed below. Has 29TH APPEARANo.—MiameI Mulkearn, who made his 20th appearance, was charged with having assaulted Mary Welsh, on Friday, the 24th ult. The complainant was going dottn Bank-street, when she met the prisoner, who said to her, "You cow, I hare been long enough waiting for you, now you mare. You should have got seven yew instead of six months. You robbed my uncle of his watcb, and have got tyro chaps doing time now." The prisoner caught hold of her by the hair of the head, threw her on the floor, kicked her, and dragged her along the tiles, causing her face to be one mass of scars.—The Bench fined the pri- soner 40s. and costs, or one month.—The prisoner : I got, that innocent. That is Mr. Hunt's doing;. he has played that card before. The prisoner's mother was denouncing the Chief Constable, who had given evidence, and had to be put out of court. YOUTHFUL INEBRIATES.—Tivo girls, apparently about 17 years of age, named Ellen Level' and Jane Flynn, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket- street, on Monday night. P.C. Edwards proved the case.— The prisoners promised amendment, and were discharged. AN OLD SCORE.—John Garvin, a puddler, was charged with being di unk and disorderly in Bridge-street, on the 20th November last.—On the evidence of P.C. Crickett, the pri- soner was fined 101. and costs, or 14 days. WEDNESDAY.-- Before Alderman Burgess, and Councillor Fairclough. A BOY BURGLAR:RIO. Wilson a lad' aged 13 years, living in Latchford was brought up Charged with having on Saturday the 18th ult., broken into the dwelling house of, Thomas Holland, and taken away. four pounds of grapes, value 2s. 6d., hind llid. in copper. The prisoner pleaded. guilty. From the etatement made by the Chief Constable it appeared that the oornplainant lives at 72,Winwick-street, and in consequence of occupying stalls in the, market, generally leaves his house and shop locked up on Siiturdays. On Saturday the 18th, complainant and his wife, and daughter went to attend the stall in the market, leaving the house locked up. On returning it was found that some one had entered through the back kitchen window and stolen about four pninds of grapes, and 11id. from the till drawer. No one was suspected until the 22nd ult., when a lad named Coyne saw the prisoner attempt to force an entrance into the complainants's premises. Prisoner was unable to do so, and on returning of the back yard wall, Coyne seized him and held him until assistance. arrived. The lad afterwards pleaded guilty to the offence, and gave the names 0 several • • the matter. The magistrates -sentenced the accomplices in . lad to one month's imprisonment, and afterwards to be kept in a reformatory for five years. Taunsnay.—Before Captain Litton and E. Milner, Esq. AN IMPORTUNATE TRAMP SENT TO GAOL.—MiChReI Brady, a tramp, was charged with 'uegging in Museum street on Wednesday night. The prisoner went to the house in Museum-street, occupied by Mr. Hesketh, and rang the bell. Mrs. Hesketh answered the bell, and the prisoner asked for relief but Mrs. Hesketh refused to relieve him. Prisoner then tried to force- himself into the house, but was prevented, and the dm* closed. He then commenced to ring the bell violently, and continued to do so for about half-an-hour, at intervals pressing ' his face against the window and making all sorts of grimaces. Mrs. Hesketh was terrified by the prisoner's conduct, and sent the servant girl for a policeman, and as she was successful in finding a constable, the prisoner was taken into custody and locked up. The Bench committed the prisoner for seven- days' hard labour.

THE COUP DE GRACE TO THE PROCEEDINGS. Mr. TIMER said it was rumoured that a Guardian had taken away some of the samples which were laid for their inspection at a recent meeting, and as many of `the Guar- dians would not like to be charged with being concerned in the affair he would like to have some information. Mr. JACKSON said he had the chairman's' authority to fetch the samples, and they did sample them. They were very good samples, and who could he better judges ? The CHAIRMAN (laughing) : This is not a Board matter. Mr. CHAMBERS : Well, they have proved themselves most faithful Guardians. The Board then rose.

ASTITON-IN-MAKERFIELD Tan DEATH or Ma. Felnt.rss.—On Monday, at noon, a large concourse of people gathered in the streets of Ashton to witness the funeral procession and interment of the late Mr. Fairless, the first in Ashton under the new Burials Act. Mr. Fairl ss came to Ashton about 12 years ago, as • assistant su veyor on the highways, but shortly afterwards became clerk to the local board, a position he has faithfully and honourably filled up to the time of his death rln addition to the immediate relatives of the deceased, the funeral was attended by the members of the local board, including the Rev. Mr. Melville and the Rev. W. Stddall. The Nonconformist burial service was read by the Rev. H. Wilson, Congregational minister, in the presence of a great many spectators. Aslrrow Cutrnen Assocwrion Snvfnex ScgooL.—The second annual distribution of prizes to the scholars con- nected with the above institution took place on Christmas Day at the Association School-room, Lodge-lane. The room was filled with an assemblage of some 130 scholars and 60 or 70 of their parents and friends. Mr. Peter Knowles, one of the vice-presidents of the Ashton branch, presided. Mr. C. Hodgkinson, on behalf of the chairman, presented the books to meritorious scholars. Those scholars who had not merited the larger prize were presented each and everyone with a Christmas card and a mince-pie, and a few who were absent through sickness were not forgotten, but had the gifts sent to them by their brothers and sisters. Ann Heyes, to her complete surprise, as also to that of all present (ex- cept the few who had been in the well-kept secret), was presented with a very handsome teachers's Bible. The inscription in the Bible was—" Presented on Christmas Day, 1880, to Miss Heyes in recognition of services voluntarily • offered to the committee twelve months ago, and up to the present faithfully rendered as the only lady teacher at the Association Sunday school." Miss Heyes having tendered' her thanks, and votes of thanks having been accorded with acclamation to the chairman for presiding, to the subscri- bers to the prize fund, to those who had cleaned and deco- rated the room, and to other friends, the proceedings con- cluded with the singing of a Christmas carol and the evening hymn "Glory to Thee," and with prayer.

lIAYDOCK ENTERTAINMENT.—On Christmas Pay, a imolai gathering of friends and relations took place at the house of Mr. Wm. Simm, Haydock, when a very agreeable day was passed. After tea an entertainment, specially got up for the occasion (after duly electing Mr. D. Sham to the chair), was com- menced by Mr. W. Simm, jun., reciting "Flight of time." Master. Geo. Makin recited, In &tit style, " The charge of the Light Brigade." " The•minstrel boy" was sung by Mr. A. James, very carefully: Then followed a dialogue, "Alex- ander and the robber," which was well rendered by Messrs. G. Makin and W. Simm, jun. Mrs. E. Dixon sang in an effective manner "My grandmother's cot." The evening I was enlivened by a tale, "Dr. Johnson's pudding," by Mr. W. Simm, and a reading in the Lancashire dialect, " Owd Croot Legs," by Mr. Geo. Makin, which caused much merri- ment. Mr. A. James again appeared with a song, "Rain- drops," well sung. A-recitation, "The bells," given by Mr. W. Simm, succeeded by Mr. GeO`: Makin with "Modern logic," was followed by Miss Sudworth sweetly and effi- ciently singing " Christgme bells." Mr. D.Simtn then gave the stirring piece, "Bate of Inkerman." Mr. John Shorn contributed a humourous song, "The captain and his bride," which was pleasantly received. Several Other songs, recita- tions, and carols by various members of the company were given, and a very pleasing and agreeable programme was gone through, much to the credit of the various persons engaged.

WINSFORD. INCHTEST AT OVER.—An inquest was held at Over by Mr. Churton on the body of a child, whose mother, Kezia Oakes, found it dead in bed,. Alter kearing the evidence, Mr. Thomas Hulse, as foreman of the jury, brought in a verdict of "Accidental death." SUCCESS OF WINSFORD STFDENTS. The Rev. C. Reader presided. Mr. H. h V. —On the same day a similar entertainment look placeat 'the Wesleyan Chapel, Swanlow-lane.. The day being very fine, ,rigbttte, fi both places were well attended, which no doubt was very gratifying to the teachers who must have worked very hard to get the children to say their pieces so well. . CHRISTMAS Tnaz.—The annual bazaar and Christmas tree was held in, the United Free Method/et Schoolroom Winsford, on Wednesday last. The room was tastefully decorated for the occasion, the work, consisting of fancy and useful articles, was laid out to the best advantage on stalls and on the large tree, the quantity being considerably in advance of formet years. A tea meeting was heIX in the afternoon, and the sale of work both preceeded and suc- ceeded it. The excellent choir enlivened the evening con- siderably. The day was very unfavourable, the rain being incessant.

payments to the said Elizabeth in case she should survive the said John ,Byrom, with power to enter upon the premises in case of failure in the said payments, And to, enjoy. the • same until they receive full satisfaction, 4tc.—Sir, John Otway thereupon lent the said John Byrom 1,000 (over and hesides the £l,OOO portion), to diScharghthe residue of the debt upon the said estate; and the said John Byrom by bargain and sale inrolled dated 17th ffeb., • 1682, conveyed all die premises of John Robinson and Robeit Hebblethwaite in trust for securing the said £l,OOO and interest; and after payment thereof the trustees to stand seised. oL the _premises till a good and perfect settlement was made of ' ,£2OO per a,nnuni (whereof .the- settled was -to be part), charged upon the premises for the jointure of the said Elizabeth his wife, and for settling, All his. estate upon such issue male as he should have by her 'with competent provision for younger children. And by indenture dated. 6 Oct., 1684, made between John Byrom of the - one part, and John Cragg, Thos. Heblethwaite. • and Robert r Sturzalter (parties to the said Recovery) of the other part, reciting the said recovery; it is declared; dm, that the re- coverers shall stand seised of the premises to the use of John , Byrom for his life, ‘nd to as much of the premises asi amount to £2OO per annum to the use of the said Elizabeth Byrom for her life; remainder of the whole to the heirs of their bodies; remainder to the right heirs of John Byrom: with a proviso that if there:should be issue both male andi female then after the death of John and his debts peid the premises (except the £2OO per annum for Elizabeth's join- j ture) to be charged, if one daughter, with £1,500, or if two or more, with opoo, to be equally divided amongst them at their respective age of 21 years or marriage," &c. We learn also that john Byrom, Esq., afterwards mort- gaged_ the premises to one Wells for .3500, which sum, and also 430,9, part of the principal money lent by Sir. John Ot- way, were still unpaid in 1705, nearly nine years after his death.. This mortgage is connected with an indenture of feoffment, dated 7th Oct., 1695, by which John Byrom of Parr Hall, Esq., conveyed to Thomas Bate of Parr, yeoman, , alibis manors, messuages, &a., of Parr, Byrom, Westleigh, Abram alias Aburgham, Hindle, Sutton, Windle and Gould- borne4 gust ; and on the 17th Oct., 1695, the said Bate conveyed the came estates to Henry Byrom of Lowton, gent., John Worsley of .Lowton, gent., Peter Corlesse and Richard Gerard, who were bound for the said John Byrom in £l,OOO to Richard Wells of Wigan, gent. In 1687 John Byrom, Esq., then living at Parr Hall in Prescot, one of the old family seats, waited upon Bishop Cartwright with 'Mr. Venables his uncle, respecting measures for recovering the advowson of St. Helen's in Frescot from the Presbyterians. John Byrom, Esq., died, we read, "in the lifetime of Adam his uncle, leaving Elizabeth his widow and six children (the youngest posthumous), three of whom died under age and unmarried, and one son and two daughters are still living" in 1705. His Will is dated at Parr, the 28th of Feb.,1695-6; and was proved at Chester by his widow an mother-in-law, Lady Elizabeth Otway, his executors, in 1696. He was buried at Winwick, the 3rd March, 1695-6. _ _ _ _

Henry Byrom, gent., only brother of John last-named,l married Catherine, daughter of John Brotherton, of Hey I Hall, Esq., but had no recorded issue by her. He resided . at Westleigh. He was living in 1682, but died towards the end of that century—certainly before 1702. Mistress Elizabeth Byrom, widew of John, married, secondly, before 1706, Robert Hedges of Chester, Esq., and, thirdly, a Mr. Hamilton, of Cheeter. She survived her first husband at least 42 years, for she was living in 1737. Her eldest daughter, Elizabeth Byrom, mauled Mr. Goulbome, of Chester; and the other surviving daughter, Catherine Byrom, was living, unmarried, in August, 1730. The story of the Byroms of Byrom is wound up by the incidents of the strange career of SAMUEL BYROM' only son and heir of the John Byrom who died in 1695-6. He was a , boy of ten years when his father died. Our MS. case states I that "Samuel Byrom, son of John and Elizabeth, being now (1704) about 19 years old, endeavours to avoid the mother's jointure, mortgages, and portions, alleging that Adanißyrorn being a lunatick when he executed the bargain and sale (in 1682), the same was void, and consequently the common Recovery was void, and that if the recovery had been good the uses thereof were not well declared, and consequently still remained in Adam." As, since the recovery, John Byrom had sold part of the premises for £5OO, if the recovery were void, the purchaser, the two mortgagees, the jointresses, and the portions for younger children would all be defeated. It was this procedure of Samuel Byrom which led to the preparation of the Case for counsel, upon which the opinions of several eminent counsel (Mr. Wm. Dobins, Mr. G. Booth, . Mr. Edward Northey, Mr. Henry Foley, and. Mr. T. Vernon) were taken in the years 1704-5. The .legal points at issue in this peculiar case are too involved to interest the general reader, and therefore we shall not cite the questions to, , and answers of counsel; except to state that the opinions , were agreed that the two daughters of John Byrom then living were entitled to their portions, and that a court of equity might decree a sale of so much of the estate as was needed to pay off the mortgage and arrears of jointure, and to raise the daughters' portions if it could not be done out of the profits of the estate in a reasonable time. Canon Parkin- son's account of the life of the last of the Byroms of Byrom, Samuel Byrom, is so interesting that we give the substance of it. Feb. 20, 1706, being then of age, Samuel Byrom executed a deed of settlement of his estates owing to a dif- ferences having arisen between himself," hie mother, Mrs. Hedges, his grandmother, Lady (Away, and his two sisters, regarding his father's marriage Settlement, as we have seen above. All the parties having secured, their rights, levied a fine, and the manor and lands were conveyed to Samuel Byrom in fee'. After struggling on a while with mortgages, the estates were finally sits.srad in 1710 Jub- 41.14, 'l7lO, Bamuet Byrom wrote to his distant kinsman, Mr. Joseph Byrom, of Manchester:—" I am surprised that you should make so many objections" (as to conditions dt purchase). "I have sold ten times the value of what you pretend to buys . , Lady Otway offered to lend me money upon the estate if I wanted it, WIT have occasion for none but to put in the lottery, and if I . sell Byrom I'll have it for that purpose." The lawyers having decided that Samuel Byrom amid alienate the Byrom estate and transfer its in- cumbrances to other property, the demesne of Byrom was conveyed to Mr. Joseph Byrom, of Manchester, on the 10th of July, 1710. From this date,Samuel Byrom led the life of a reckless spendthrift. In. 1729, when he would be 44 years old, he published a tract, entitled :—"An Irrefragable Argument, fully proving that to discharge .Grreat Debt is less injury and more reasonable than to discharge Small Debts. Humbly offered to the Legislature, By &autism BYROM, late of Byrom and. Par in the County Palatine of Lancaster, Esq., and now a Prisoner within the walls of the. Fleet Prison, London, &c. London, printed for, the benefit of the Author, 1720." It is dedicated to the Duke of Dorset, and the writer reminds the Duke that when at Westminster School he (4yrom) had boarded for many years in the same house with his Grace. At that time he had, he says, a competent estate in Lanca- shire; but being iltintroduced Mtis the world, and soon fall- ing into the'hands of sharpers and gamesters, his estate was diminished and his reputation lost: Reduced to want, aban- doned lay his relations, slighted by those who had obtaiued his property; he fell a victim to usury, villainy, and malice; and being deceived by an attorney, was tricked into prison, where he must have perished if he had not been repeatedly , relieved by the Duke of Dorset. He adds :—" It would be more feasible for me to wash a blackmoor white than to pay 1 my debts; and must I be starved to death and kept in prison for no other reason but because / am a gentleman and had once an estate? 0 horrid and monstrous!" In Junesl73s, Dr. Byrom, of Kersall, was interesting himself on behalf et "beau Byrom" (as the wastrel Samuel was styled), who had then got out of the Fleet. The doctor suggested he should go to Parr H all in this county, but he was not willing. In April, 1736, he was in London, and had "stopped the Prince," petitioning for help. Dr. Byrom in August, 1735, wrote of him :—" I was in frequent apprehension of his perishing in the streets of London." His mother and aunt, ' Mrs. Otway, still sometimes relieved him, but to no purpose; ' ' and in February, 1739, Dr. Byrom wrote I wish I could do him any service, but as I have not many hopes at present. I wait till I have." Canon Parkinson concludes :—" When, where, or how he died is unknown. The seventeenth in lineal descent from Henry de Byrom, living in the 19th Edward 11., born to inherit wealth and nurtured in luxury, squandered in a very few years the large estates of his , respectable and provident ancestors, and died a beggar." But may not the circumstance that this unfortunate scion of an ancient house found his estates at the outset heavily overweighted by jointures, settlements, and mortgages, which even the most prudent of heirs might with difficulty., have discharged, afford, if not palliation, at least some ex- planation of his unhappy lapse into heedless and improvi- dent habits? The details we have presented show that the fortunes of the Byroms, what with the premature death in battle of one member, the lunacy of other members, the long ! minority of other heirs, and the difficulty of adjusting all claims, had begun to droop more than fifty years before the succession of that last representative whose fatal weakness hurried on the catastrophe.
