. _ Tuesns-v.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage. Aermearn Batumi. ASSAtIa ON A LABOITRER.---A fall, powerful-looking man named Patrick Fitzsimmons, a labourer, living in Queen-at, was charged on remand with un- lawfully wounding John O'Neill, who lives in the same street. Complainant said he was a! labourer, and lived at No. 16, , Queen-street. On Saturday night, the 18th inst., about ten o'clock, be went into the prisoner's house. The prisoner lived in the same street—within a few doors. He lodged with the prisoner some time ago, and he went in to have a chat with him. Be remained there about 20 minutes before anything took place, and they had nothing in the place to drink. The disturbance commenced by his having some words with a man named Patrick Downs, who was also in the house. The prisoner took Downs's part, and said that lie (witness) had used the word informer. No sooner had Fitzeiremons matie this remark than he caused kiln to fall upon the floor. He could not say whether the primmer knocked or pushed him down, but whilst he was upon the floor ha kicked him several times on the face and the back of the bead. He distinctly remembered receiving three kicks—two on the face and one on the back of his laud. He Med a great deal, after which he became insensible. One of the kicks was on his eyebrow. On recovering consciousness he found he waleha his bed at his lodgings; having been carried out of the prisoner's house. He never struck the prisoner, or gave him any provocation. He was not drunk, but he had had four glasses of beer and some gingerbeer. Be did not remember the doctor dressing his wounds that night, but when he awoke the next morning be be discovered they had been tstitched and dressed. Dr. McLennan had attended him since, and he had been confined to his braise and unable to follow his employment. He was not yet able to go to his work.—ln cross-examination, the com- plainant admitted that he had 1501:063 words with Patrick Downs. It was quite true that be pulled his coat off to fight with Downs, when the Prisoner ordered him out of the house and said that was not a place to fight. Tlaeprisoner, did not, however, give him time to go out. He did not tarn round to Downs and strike him.—ln re-cross- examination, the complainant said the prisoner had clogs on at the • time he k:cked him, and the ejoge produced were similar to those he :wore at the time.— Clirke, of No. 5, Queen-street, said that on Was night; of Saturday, the 18th alt., at about ten o'clock, she went to the prisoner's house, having been sent for by his wife. On opening the door she saw the prisoner kick- ing O'Neill, who was lying on the floor. She saw him kick the man twice on the face, and also on the back part of the bead. The prisoner was standing by a table at the time. There was a large pool of blood on the floor. He heard the prisoner say that if O'Neill aid not go out of the house he would take his life. She went to O'Neill's landlady to tell her what had happened. O'Neill was at this time insensible, and she observed wounds on the back of his head. She and the other woman removed the complainant to his own lodgings.—Esther Lerner, wife of Patrick Lerner, of No. 16, Queen- street, saidithat on the night of the 18th ult., the lea' witness came into her house, and, from what she said to her, she went with hej to the prisoner's house. The com- plainant was lying on the floor, on which there was much blood, and there were several wounds upon his head, from which he was bleeding. She spoke to O'Neill', who knew her voice, and asked her to assist him to rise. She and the last witness, and another woman, helped the man into his own lodgings. She saw the prisoner near the kitchen door, and he had on his feet nothing but his stockings. The prisoner told her that the complainant had called him "a informer," and he would neither allow him nor any other person to call him by such names in his own house. Two or three men then went for A doctor, and Mr. McLen- nan came shortly afterwards, and dressed his wounds. The complainant had been confined to his house since, and in bed most of the time.—Dr. McLennan said that on the night of the 18th ult. he was called to see the complainant, at about a quarter past eleven. He found him bleeding pro- fusely from several wounds on the face and scalp. There was a lacerates wound, about two inches long, on the left eyebrdw, a small incised wound on the outer part of the eyebrow, a punctured wound on the back of the head, and both complainant's eyes were black.—He was else very weak from loss of blcod ; and some of his wounds were of a dangerous character. They were inch as would be produced by kicks from a clog,snd had the appearance of having been caused by some thing of that kind. Extreme violence must have been used to in- filet such wounds,—a fall would not have caused them. He stitched the wound on the eyebrow and dressed the others. He had attended the man since, and for three days he was in a dangerous state.—Complainant was still unable to follow his employment.—P.C. Laing said that on the night of the assault after it had taken place, he went to the prisoner's house in Qtmen-street, and found much blood upon the floor. He told the prisoner to put on his coat and come along with him, on a charge of unlawfully wounding O'Neil. Prisoner made no reply. He again charged him at the police station, and prisoner saia "I am not guilty of kicking; I had no clogs on at the time." Fitzsummons, on being formally sbarged, pleaded not guilty.—He was committed for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions. On making application for bail, the police strongly opposed his request. —Mr. Gossage I certainly shall not allow bail. The prisoner was then re- moved. * Wensresuev.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell (chairman) Mr. F. H. Gossage, Mr. George Pilkington, and Mr. Fletcher.

DEFRAUDING THE LONDON AND NOETII-WESTRIZN RAIL- WAY Ca—Henry Jones, plumber, was charged by the Lon- don and North Western Rally Co, with having travelled, on the 13th inst., from Liverpool to Widnes without having previously paid his fare, and with intent to avoid payment. —Mr. Ferrand(frem the office of Mr. Preston, the company's -solicitor, Lime-street), appeared to prosecute. During the bearing of the case, Mr. Fletcher, who is a director of the sompany, retired from the Bench. Mr. Sansom, the station starter, at Widnes, said that about half-past eleven o'oclock if the forenoon of the 13th inst., be was called to the ticket sollector's office, where be found a dispute going en between the defendant and the collector. -Jones was trying to cony vince the collector that he had only bees on the platform for 116 e purpose of seeing some one awarby train. He ascer- tained that a witness then in court had travelled with the young man from Edge Bill to Widnes.—Mr. Scrimgeour, eontractor, of St. Helens, said that on the morning in ques- tion he came by train from Liverpool, and the prisoner got in at Ede Hill, after being told, in answer to a question, that the train was going to Widnes. The Chairman said defendant was liable to a fine of 40e., and if any more cases ef a similar character were brought before them, they would , be compelled to inflict the maximum fine. He would have to pay a tine of 10s. and costs, or in default, be sent to gaol for fourteen days, with hard Ist:mt.—J. B. Foulkes, for- merly employed in the goodsyard of theeame eompany, was *barged with having, on the 15th -ult., travelled from Liverpool to Widnes without having paid his fare, and with ieitent to &fraud the company. A second and similar aharge was also preferred against him as to the following day. Mr. Ferrand said that- two years ago the defendant was in the employ of ,the company, and, consequently, knew most of the ire-and-outs with travelling npon the line. He and many others had for some time boen in the habit of travelling from Liverpool or Edge Hill, to Widnes by the last train at night, and passing the porter who was eollecting by giving him twopence or threepence or paying for him something. On the 15th inst a porter named Nqon was on duty, when the defendant came in by the 10-50 p.m. knin from Lime-street, and on going down stairs to the entrance where he was standing, the defendant was asked Ala his ticket. .11e then said he had not had time to get a bottle that night, but he would put the matter all right on another occasion. Noon answered " What! a bottle. I don't want any bottle of you. I want your ticket." De- fendant then gave him some money, and on going into the effice to enter it, he found it ;was only threepence, and temarked to himself, that he ehould report the man. iHe told Mr. Sansom, and on the following night he was told to keep a look out for the defendant. He saw him go to Liverpool by the 7-34 train. On defendant returning by train to the station, he raw defendant get out of a third Allan carriage. The station master was on duty to and on the man coming up to him (witness) be did not give any ticket, but simply put his finger into his land. He said, "That won't do, and the station master, who had been watching the transaction, stopped the de- lendant.—The porter (Noon) and Mr. Saneom were called, and corroborated this statement.—Foulkes, in defence, said that on the night of the 15th tilt., when found coming off the platform, he had not come from Liverpool, but had been son the premises upon some business. On the second night le had not time to get his ticket at Liverpool, and on arriving at Widnes he offered the money for the fare, but it was not accepted.—The Chairman said this was a much worse case than the one with which the magistrates had hist dealt, as it was quite evident that defendant had taken advantage of the special knowledge he had acquired whilst In the company's service. He had also aggra.vated his *Hence by endeavouring to corrupt the porter by putting money into his hand to bribe him to condone the offence. Defendant would have to pay 20s. and costs in each case, or, in default of payment, be .sent to gaol one naonth.—De- Indent had a total of 1,2 ge. to pay. THE TOPERS' Lter.—Michael Holden and Thomas Clon- seamon, neither of whom appeared, were each Bald 55.-and Goats for haying been drunk and disorderly at Mersey View, and wishing to fight.—Austin Dennett had a like snai and eoets to pay for having been drunk and guilty of shouting and swearing at Appleton. ,village, on the 18th ult.—John Stiinn and Michael McCabe,for having been drunk and dis- orderly in Victoria-street, on the 24th ult., were fined ss. and costs, on the evidence •01 P.C. Stott.—On the evidence of the same officer, John Connor had ss. and coste.to pay fbr drunkenness in High-street, on the 24th tilt.—Ami Shaivt a tramp, was fined a like sum for having been drunk in an entry in Camline-street, that morning. P.C. Stott gave *ewein this case. , 'dense ULASSES BROM THE RAILWAY HOTEL /di:ellen, a young woman, who was convicted of stealing et'ale in December, 1875, pleaded guilty to taking two tambler glasses from the Railway Hotel, Victoria-road, on Monday event- os. Robert Turton, the barman, missed the glasses, and gave information to Mr.-Jamee Davies, estate agent, who is in charge of the house at present, and he gave her in custody to P.C. Timperley, to whom she denied being •y of the charge.—Prisoner ate next charged. with Clieraking the window of her cell and a large board in her red.—The Chairman wild she would not be proceeded against for the wilful damage, but in the case of theft she would be fined 10e. and costs, or, in default di payment, be sent to gaol 14 days. Atuynirg WIDNES CASE OF thar.savvt-riat Worarmsrat. —Hugh c onjey and James Farrell, two young men were aharged, in custody' with unlawfully wounding 'James Illosmloy, of Moes Bank, on the 24th ult.—The Police-In-

spector said that Farrell, the younger of the prisoners, had been locked up on the information of the brother of the in- jured man, who now declined to say anything aualist him. He had, therefore, to ask for his discharge.—Farrell was then released from the dock.—Bridget Gormley, wife of James Gormley, or Elizabeth-greet, Moss Bank, said that on Christmas Eve she saw the prisoner go up to the com- plainant and threaten to knock his brains out. Some few minutes afterwards, she observed prisoner knock the complainant down with something that he had in his hand. She could not say whether the instrument broke when the prisoner struck the man. They had to take complainant to Dr. Ryan, and he had been confined tobed since.—P.C.Strick- land said he apprehended the prisoner on Monday morning awl took him into the presence of the injured DUD, who said to him "Yen are the man who struck me over the eye.—Mr. Ryan, surgeon, stated that on the 25th instant he was called to see the prisoner at about one o'clock in the morning, fie found him suffering from an injury to the right eye, which had apparently been inflicted by a blunt instrument. The wound was a serious one, and the place greatly swollen and disceloured.—ln answer to a question from the Inspector of Police, the witness admitted that the ball of the man's eye was broken, and he feared he would lose his sight.—The Chairman: And why did you not tell us that before? You seem very unwilling to give evidence. --In answer to furtherquestions, the witness admitted that the man was still in a dangerous state.—The prisoner, who is a very powerful looking man, urged that the case ought to be taken that day, as his witnesses were in attendance.— The Chairman said the magistrates could not hear the case in the absence of comialainant, and he reminded the priso- ner that if the injured man were to die, the charge against him would immediately resolve itself into one of a very serious nature.—The prisoner was remanded until Wednes- day nest. .

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. • - The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guar- dians was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday last. Present :—Tbe Rev. Canon Barclay (in the chair), Rev. Canon Dodd, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Ashton, H. Lowe, T. Andrews, W. Whittaker, T. Norman, W. Whitlow, W. Jackson, J. Midwood, J. Darbyshlre, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). TEH mesm's REPORT. . _ _ -

The Magma (Mr. R. Jones) reported 161 in the House, as against 176 in the corresponding week of last year. Nine vagrants were relieved during the week, of whom seven were men and two women. In attendance at the workhouse school there were 21 boys and 28 girls; and 12 boys and 25 girls were receiving industrial training. Out-door relief had been administered to 643 persons, at a cost of £6l 6s. Id. (appor- tioned as follows :—Tinncorn, £34 18s; Frodsharn, £l5 38. Td.; and‘ Badworth, £l2 4s. 8c1.), as compared with 680 persons relieved at a cost of £66 Os. 7d. in the corresponding week of last year. - -CIIRISVEAS AT THE WORKHOUSE. The Minim also reported that the inmates had their usual Christmas dinner of roast beef and potatoes in extra quantities, together with an unlimited supply of plum pudding and half a pint of ale each, the children having milk instead of ale. For supper the inmates were regaled with bread and cheese and ale, the children having milk as before ; and by the Board's orders the smokers had two ounces of tobacco each, instead of their usual quantity of one ounce; while snuff-takers had also double allowance, and the non-smokers an orange vitt]. The children were treated with toys from a Christmas tree, the toys being gived by Mr. George Razleharat, and the tree by Mr. Peter Tickle. APPOINTMENT ,D 1 ASSISTANT ItELIEVING OFFICER.
On the motion of Mr. Tnostss NORMA/C, Inspector Hollingsworth was appointed assistant relieving officer at Runcorn, in the place of Inspector Dutton resigned.

ALLEGED EXTRiVAOANCE BY TUE MASTER AND MATRON. Mr. Lows said be had a complaint which he wished to lay before the Board. That day he artived at the House rather earlier than usual, and when at the stables one of the men came to feed Mr. Jones's pony and brought a dish of as nice hot potatoes as he ecer saw put on a dish. He found on making enquiries that the potatoes cams out of the House. He called the attention of a carter who was there to them, and who said he was a ratepayer and helped to pay for the potatoes. It was a great shame that Mr. Jones, the master of the House, should feed his pony on potatoes which belonged to the Union. The pony was the master's property, and he ought to pay for its keep. Mrs. Jones doubted his word, and said what was given to the pony was potato peelings, but he told her they were good potatoes. They had been peeled and boiled, and smoked on the dish, and were such as Guardians would have on their own tables. • _ . .

REV. Clorox DODD believed the matron was prepare with a defence, and, if called before the Board, she would be able to give an explanation of the matter. Mr. Nommen thought a case of this sort ought to be cleared up from beginning to end,—(hear, bear)—because it was a very serious charge to be brought against a workhouse master, •

The Mavacits was then called into the room, and in reply to the Chairman, said to her knowledge the pony had never had a potato. They were potato peelings which were given to the pony as the pigs would not eat them. She had had to thtow the peelings on the midden for three weeks. Mr. Nonstats: Are you sure no potatoes have been boiled and taken to the pony? .

The MATRON: I am sue there has not been a potato boiled unless somebody has done it with a bad will, Mr. Norman. I can't say anything about that. Mr. Lowis thought before the matron went away be should say they were not peelings; and he did not think there were any peelings amongst them. The MATRON said, if the Board would believe her, to her knowledge there was never such a thing sea potato given to the pony. There might be somebody bad enough to set them a trap; but she was certain neither she nor her hus- band knew anything about it. Mr. Low's: I did not say that you did..

A womamwho was engaged in-the kitchen, was called in, and she stated that two potatoes fell in the &aril on the tictor, and as they were not fit for anybody to eat they were put on one side for the pony. Mr. NORMAN: Have you ever done that before? The Wostax: No, sr; I never have; but I know horses are fond of potatoes. Mr. Nonmax : That is not the question. Have on ever given the horse potatoes before? ' The Woman': No, Mr ;. only potato peelings. A man named Huxley, who took charge of the pony, said he generally fed the pony on corn and potato peelings. He gave the pony, that day, two potatoes and a half that were left, and that was the first time he had given it potatoes, as the matron had given him strict orders to take only potato peelings. Mr. LOWE: Yeti know very well there were more than 2i potatoes. Horxram : I beg your pardon, there,were no more than 2. Mr. Lowly Well I leave it to you; but you know better. The Ow/wax : Well, Mrs. Jones, it shows the necessity of being very careful. The MATRON: Well, I really am very careful, and most anxious not to do wrong. The CHAniarew : It shows the necessity of looking after your servants, who may play tricks without any meaning at all. The MA7yRON It is not the first time they have tried to ' do us injury. Mr. Lows Ido not think it will do them any injury; it is the ratepayers. The MATRON: If you were as careful or any guardian on the Board was as careful of the ratepayers' -money, things would not go very far Wrong: (Hear, hear.) We consider the ratepayers as well as anybody else, Rev. J. W. N. TANNER said Mr. and Mrs. Jones had had the management of that House's() many years tbat it was quite a criterion there would be no extravagance; and he thought it was a very injurious accusation which had been brought against them. The Board knew they economised as much as they could: and if the Board looked at the cost of any ,other Union they would find a great difference. There was no Union conducted with greater economy', and , they had to thank Mr. anefltfrs. Jones for it.. If two and a half potatoes had been given to the pony they had been given by the servants. Mr. Nonster said the matter had been entirely cleared up in his opinion. If Mr. Lowe and every other Guardian attended as well to their duty as Mr. Jones did to the house, there would not be much to complain of. The CHAIRMAN At the same time I must say Mr. Lowe is perfectly instified from what has passed before in bring- ing the matter forward. Mr. LOwa thought the remarks of Mr. Tanner were very disgraceful to him as a Guardian. What were they sent there for but to look after the interests of the ratepayers ? He could honestly say there were more than two and a half potatoes; but if the Guardiang were not to speak when they saw anything, and Mr: Tanner and Mr. Norman were to throw slights on thetn; the sooner they stayed at Vonid the better. He denied what they said in tote. Rev. Canon DODD quite agreed that Mr. Lowe was justi- fied in bringing the matter forward; but there was such a thing as evidence, and Mr. Lowe was entirely unsupported by evidence. On the contrary, it was all against him. TREAT TO TEE POOR PEOPLB AT ST. HELP.NS. On Christmas day, about 100 poor, lame, and blind persons sat down to a tea provided for them in the Victoria Hall, Crop- -N Hill, Sf. Helens. .A similar treat was provided two

per's years ago,and this year Mr. W., Barker was mainly instru- mental in promoting this most praiseworthy object. Old men and women on crutches, and the blind people mingling together, and enjoying themselves at tea presented a strange, though grand spectacle, and every effort was made to add to their pleasure. The tables were presided over by Mrs. Green, the Misses Kerr,liall, E. Pye and Polly P7e. After the tea an entertainment was held, and sacred pieces were sung by the children. Addresses were delivered hy the Rev. Charles Green, minister at the Victoria Hall, Mr. Barker, Mr. Andrews, and Mr. Simpson; and Mrs. Mellor, a blind lady, contributed several concertina solos. A most pleasant evening was spent, and the halt, the maimed, and' the blind expressed themselves in terms of gratitude to those who had been at so much trouble and expense in contribu- ting to their happiness.

A committee was appointed to consider the matter. not FLOSISRAOR OF BELFRY : PETITION PROM THE - RATEPAYERS. - Mr. MIDITOOD presented the following petition on behalf of the ratepayers in Relsby :—" Helsby sewerage.—To the Chairman and members of the Sanitary Authority, Runcorn Union,—Rev. sir, and gentlemen,—We, the undersigned, owners of property, and ratepayers of the township of Helsby, beg most respectfully to represent to you our deep regret that, at your last meeting, you should have decided to carry out a scheme, of 'sewerage here, about which we know so little, six! concerning -which neither plans, pro- bable cost, nor ultimate design, had been brought under our nodes, and, considering that only five out of eleven mem- bers who were present voted on that occasion, you will not, we trust, deem us unreasonable in soliciting it your hands a further considerktion of the circumstances in which we are placed. For your information but for the new members es- pecial ly,we beg to remind you that some time ago,when the nu!. sance was first complained of, adeputation of your body, with your Inspector, kindly came to Helsby, and saw the locality for themse:ves. The scheme which the ratepayers had agreed upon was explained to them, and in all its particu- lars they gave, it their entire approval; and subsequently a second deputation from your Board came over, with a similar result. About the same period a memorial from us was presented to the Sanitary Authority en the subject, the final impression we entertained (mistaken or not) being that the scheme was adopted, and would at once have been executed by you. The scheme itself was very simple, and had the additional advantage of being comparatively inex- pensive. It was to deepen the ditch running from Collier's Square, and Moss Cottages and Ellam's farm, to admit socket pipes of sufficient diameter taking them along past Youd's cottage to a spot in his garden, where a capacious tank wonld be built as a receptacle for all the sewage matter; such of the solid aa might by chance ilnd its way into the pipes would be deposited in this tank, while the affluent water would be ;allowed to flow along the ditch, as it as done from time immemorial. A small yearly allowance was to be paid to Mr. Youd for allowing the tank to be made on his property, and he was to undertake to keep ist tht cleanedains dpiinag n wouldt ohuatt at the tbt be efficacious orderwas catoci oohufaasnvy deof uoabrrne eetnhn com- mittee will readily judge of our surprise when we learned that it had been set aside, inspector. aPerluryiredi newooseut Believingnyn ed adopted thatnd er —one respecting which the ratepayers of Helsby knew next to nothing Knowing the disposition of the commit- tee to always do what was best, and-their anxiety to trench as lightly as possible upon the pockets of the ratepayers. we respectfully ask that you rescind the former order and adopt this original scheme which will cost little, not more,perhaps than some MO or £25, and will completely remedy the nui- sance, and be satisfactory to everybody concerned; and fur- ther that you give authority for its speedy execution the oast to be charged upon the proper rate. With this we hand, for the information of the committee, a plan of the locality, showing the line of the ancient ditch, the cottage property contigous thereto, with the natural descent, and other points necessary for the proper understanding of the subject. —We are, 'Rev. sir, and gentlemen, very faithfully yours." Then followed the signatures of 123 ratepayers. Mr. M/DWOOD also banded the chairman a letter from Mr. James Reynolds, who, he said, first complained of the nui- sance, 'stating that he had seen the memorial respecting the drainage of Helsby, and thought if the sewage of Collin's square and its vicinity, as proposed, was carried into Yond's garden, it would obviate the nuisance. The CLERK, in reply to Mr. Darbyshire, said the scheme which the Authority adopted at the last meeting was part of one which was passed in 1874 by Mr. Greenwood, the Authority's surveyor. It was very desirable, when any special business was coming before the Authority, that due notice should be given to the clerk, so that he could be pre- pared with all the particulars. The matter had been going on since 1874. At the last meeting he hal all particulars in the matter at hand, but on the present occasion he had no knowledge that the matter would be a ;ain under discussion, and was not prepared with the necessary books, papers, &c. If Mr. Midwood or the Helsby ratepayers [Mr. Midwood : It is the Helsby ratepayers] had given notice to the clerk that the matter would be again brought forward he would have been prepared with-all information. MrkMIDWOOD then gave notice that at the next meeting he aliSuld move that the resolution which the Authority passed at their last meeting in reference to the sewerage of Mislay- be rescinded. THE STATE OF THE APPLETON ROADS. Rev. Canon DODD asked who was responsible for making good the roads at Appleton, which had been disturbed by the sewerage operations. The CLERK stated that the district surveyor ought to see that the work was done. Rev. Canon Donn said the roads had been left in a dis- graceful state, and something ought to be done to have them put in proper condition. The CLERK remarked that he had received four com- plaints during the past fortnight respecting the roads named. . , This was all the business before the Authority.

TOPERS.—EIIen McDonald, a middle-aged woman, had ss. and ss. 4d. costs to pay for being drunk in Church-street, on the 24th ult. P.C. Kelly proved the case.—Henry Jaekson and Samuel Watson were charged with having been 'drunk and disorderly in Granville-street, on the 26th tilt. Sergeant Handford stated that en the previous night, about 11 o'clock, the two defendants were drunk and fighting in the street named, and they caused a great crowd to collect. Defen- dants, who pleaded guilty, had each 10s. fine and ss. 4d. costs to pay, or in default be imprisoned 14 days.—Timothy Bryant, a young man, was charged with similar behaviour, on the 18th ult. P.C. Cooper said that about half-past ten o'clock at night, the defendant made a disturbance in Wee. ton village, and cursed and swore very much. Superinten- dent Williamson said that on tha night of the day when the defendant received his summons, he went to the , house of the constable who had served it, and was so violent tbat•he alarmed the man's wife very much. The Bench Said the defendant bad aggravated his offence by going to the officer's house, and he would have to pay 20s. and 10s. tkl. costs, or go to gaol one month. The hearing of several cases was adjourned. Tarmsuev.—Before Mr. S. B. Chadwick.

_ BEGGING.—Henry Johnson, a rivetter, who said he came from Manchester, was charged with begging In Bridge- street, on Wednsday night.—P.C. Bossons stated that he found the prisoner begging in a shop, and on searching him, three pawn tickets—one for a watch—and fivepence were found upon him.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for seven days with hard labour. (aged 1.3) and Joseph,Wils,on (aged).,) were chary -With stealing 30s: from the-till of -Andrew Brown, drugg t,. Bridge-street, the previous night. Sergeant Walley that he had been concerned in the robbery, and said that some of he, money was concekled under.a hedge bank. The place was searched, and 15s. Of the money found.—The prieonere were remanded until Monday.

After dinner a concert was held in the assembly rooms adjoining the hotel, at which there were several hundred persons present. During tea, deceased seemed in a gloomy state, and remarked that he had had some tremble with his work that day. Deceased and his wife had no quarrel that day, and her stepmother never went out of the house that night. In answer to several questions, witness said that she heard more voices than one on the bridge about mid-night. It seemed like as if there was some one scuffling. Rebecca Walker, the wife of the deceased was again called, and in answer to the coroner said she had no idea how the deceased got into the canal. He had no cause for troubles as she never heard that he had gone wrong with his employers. She had no suspicion of any foul play con- nected with the affair. She did not suggest or insinuate that some one in the neighbourhood had pushed the deceased In the canal. The Coroner said .he believed the deceased had come to his death in an accidental manner, and the only verdict they could return was an open verdict. There was nothing to show how he riot in the canal and he thought they must divest their minds of everything in the way of suspicion. Mr. Garnett, one of the jurors, said that the enquiry had lasted a long time, but they had satletled themselves as to the nature of deceased's death. The Coroner said jurymen nowadays were too suspicious of cases which they could not fathom completely. A great English law to regard everything as an accident until proved to the contrary was very much disregarded. There may have been rumours afloat respecting the manner in which the deceased met his death, but the evidence had shown that such rumours wcre entirely unfounded. They could do nothing else than bring in an open verdict. The jury then returned a yerdictio the above effect. Several of the jurymen were of opinion that a present- ment, to the effect, that the railway comparfy provide a better crossing to the house where the deceased lived, should be added to the verdict, but the Coroner thought it quite unnecessary.

HIGH LEGIT TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. in accordance with a custom observed for; a long time, the members and friend's df the above SoclUy attended at the house of Mr. David 'Okell, High Legh, on Christmas Day„ when a convivial meeting was held. Mr. George Okell, the, oldest teetotaller present, was -deputed to the chair, and hel delivered an address bearing upon the difficulties the h p',aoneers of the temperance movement had to encounter, and urging upon all the importance of signing the terapertnce pledge.—Mr. R. A. Naylor of Thelwall, also addressed`tlie meeting, and said it gave him ple.auure end satisfaction to he a worker in the great temperance cause: 'The movement in High Legh had been begun and continued ,by the Okell family for a generation, and looking at the meeting that evening,which in point of numbns would compare favour- ably with any of-ita predecessors he had attended, he could not say their labours had been in vain. Although, through the action of benevolent landowners, public-houses and; beershops had beep probibited in several parishes in the immediate neighbourhood, still there were others on the outskirts of the distxict *which they had to guard against ; I and he hoped the time was not far distant when the number of these places would be further redubed, sci as to make it easy for them to do right and difficult to do wrong.—Mr.' John Naylor also addressed the meeting, and strongly advised all the ladles present who had not yet 'become' teetotallers to sign the pledge that night. He believed the young ladies would increase their matrimonial value by 80 doing by at least 50 per e:ent.; for they lived in days when every available corner grocery was converted into a plate him that beer and other intoxicating drinks' for the sale of intoxicating liquors, and some of his friends ohcacdasassure d appeared- in their family bills as "groceries" and "dittos. He advised all young men to 'form an acquaintance with those who were teetotiillers in preference. to those who were drinkers, as they would ffild that to be the the evening, and a pleasant entertainment' best course in the end.—An excellent programme was gone hwidth a voteuring of thanks to the chairman, -' - cthlorcoeudg

Mr. Hartley spoke to the defendant, who was asked whether he could give any explanation as to the vouchers not being accurate ; and he at first denied, but one of the Guardians had said that he acknowledged it. Mr. Swift here interposed, and asked that Mr. Fidler might be sent out of the room to the other witnesses, as he was the only person who had made the statement public. Mr. Fidler then left the court. Mr. Seger (continuing) said that whether any admission was made by the defendant or not still the tickets had been altered, and it was perfectly clear the prisoner had obtained more money than he was entitled to. Mr. Swift called the attention of the Bench to the circum- stance that there were twelve summonses, and he would wish Mr. Seger to select those summonses in particular upon which he was going to proceed. Mr. Seger ultimately selected the summonses for stealing is. on the ith September, and is. on the let December. Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Prescot Board of Guar- dians, then gave evidence, and said one of his duties was to examine the accounts of the relieving officers. He was examined by Mr. Segar at considerable length, and gave evidence bearing out the statement of the prosecuting counsel. Cross-examined by Mr. Swift: Witness said Prescott was supported by very good testimonials when he made appli- cation for the post of relieving officer. He had a general testimonial, signed by the leading gentlemen of the town. Up to the last he was a very active and deser7ing officer; and at the meeting of the Guardians at which that prosecu- tion was directed many of the Guardians expressed their surprise that there should be any charge against him. He believed he was a hard-working, industrious officer, and that by his industry and attention and his enquiry into cases he saved the Union a considerable sum of money during his term of office. For some time before the 18th December he had been doing the work of two officers—he believed from the latter end of August, his colleague, Mr. Wensley, being off duty in consequence of illness. There was reasonable ground for belief that he would receive some compensation for his extra services. Mr. Swift examined the application and report books, and. asked Mr. Hartley if all the writing on a certain page was done by one man. Mr. Hartley replied that it was ; whereupon Mr. Swift pointed out to the Bench that there was a great difference in some of the figures, and handed up the books for the magistrates' inspection. The magistrates said there was a difference in the figures, though they believed they were all made by the same ' person. In answer to Mr. Swift, witness said that in the ninth week of the quarter ended 29th September out of a total payment by the defendant for relief of £62 17s. 7d. the Board were charging the defendant with having misappro- priated Is, On the Ist December he (witness) asked defen- dant what he had paid to Wilcock, and he said "£3 45.," and that had proved to be correct. He also asked him what be had paid to Massey, and be replied "£2." He had mad° enquiries, and Massey's account agreed with what defen- dant had said. The defendant produced tickets amounting to £2, but those tickets showed they were not paid on that particular Saturday (Ist December), though, as against the Guardians, defendant had not taken credit for them before. div.head: CHRISTMAS FESTIVITIES AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: CHRISTMAS FESTIVITIES AT ST. HELENS.
LOWE HOUSE.

Special services wer-e—ceieUraiied-a-t-tbis church on Christ- mas Day, commencing at the early hour of six o'clock in the morning, and proceeding every half hour up till ten o'clock. Solemn High Mass was sung at eleven o'clock by ; one of the German Fathers, assisted by a deacon and sub- deacon, and a forcible sermon was preached by the Rev. Father Turner. . The music was rendered by the choir in their usual manner, and Mr. Lawrence officiated at the organ. The offertory piece was, of courser the beautiful and very seasonable hymn, " Adeste Fideles." At most of the services there were very fair attendances. There was no Mass on the Eve of Christmas, nor was there any evenin% service on Christmas Day. The church was very neatly decorated, and of course a " crib " had been erected. HOLY CROSS CEGIRCH.

This place of worship had been as usual prettily decorated in a manner symbolic of the joyful time, and the High Altar stood out in striking-contrast to its appearance a day or two previous, haying received close attention to its adornment. The church was also hung round with very pretty bannerettes, which relieved its usually somewhat somlire appearance. A beautiful "crib" has been con- structed in the left transept, and is a work which has evidently taken up both time and expense. There was no midnight Mass, but service commenced at six o'clock on the morning of Christmas Day, at which early hour a large con- gregation assembled to attend Mass and listen to the singing of the Christmas hymns, by the children, who were accom- panied on the harmonium by Miss Morris. Services- went on every, succeeding half' hour •up to ten o'clock, and at eleven o'clock solemn High Mass was sung by a priest deacon, and sub-deacon, the large chinch being almustfilled. An excellent sermon was preached by Father Cardwell, front the text "Glory be to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will." On this occasion Gonnod's grand work the ".Messe Solennelle," was sung in, its entirety by a full choir in a manner well worthy of conituendation. The offertory piece was the. Christmas hymn, " Ade* Fideles," and at the conclusion tif the service Handel's chorus (from the" Messiah.") "Per unto us a child is brim," was rendered. There was evening service at this church at which Father Dignain delivered an eloquent discourse taking as his text," Peace on earth to men of gopd will." On Sun- day eretting, • the• last Sunday in the year, a solemn "Te Deum " was sung in thanksgiving for the benefits of the past year. The selectied was Romberg's grand "Te Deum," and full justice was done to it by the choir, the tones of the the, fine organ being well brought-by Mr. Unsworthothe organist.

MR. &MINNIE& M.P., AND HIS CONSTITUENTS: (F-forn the Salford ireekly News.) - - The member for Warrington, Mr. J. G. McMinnies—the gentleman who displaced the great local brewer who some years since became one of the seven baronets created by Lord Beaconsfield as the reward of his silent parliamentary support of the Tory party for twenty years—addressed his constituents on Wednesday evening. The summary of Mr. McMinnies' speech, as published in the Manchester Exa- miner on Thursday, excellent as it is, conveys but an im- perfect notion of The speaker's political capacity and the breadth and depth of the culture which is sometimes com- pitiblo with a life of extraordinary commercial industry and success. Mr. McMinnies is one of the political veterans who during the life of the Anti-corn Law League was per- sonally identified with that beneficent and triumphant con- federation. He was one of those courageous Lancashire cOtton lords Who helped to keep alive the sacred fires which gave force and inspiration to the "League," and finally lighted it to victory. Nor is the member for Warrington by any means the sole instance where the chiefs of Lanes- shire trade took their natural place in the House of Com- mons at the last general election. In this borough we have our President of the Board of Trade, over the Irwell we have Mr. Slagg, elsewhere we have Mr. Summers, Mr. Briggs, Mr. Thomaseon, and other prominent Lancashire men, all of ,whom, in a few short month, have furnished to the political world striking testimonk of their illness for the places of service and honour decreed to them at the polling booths.

Mr. MeMinnies' speech contained a few sentences of especial power and value. He said he believed that the present Government deserved the support of every true Liberal in this country, and he pointed out with what heroic resolution the Government had Immediately ad- dressed itself to the work awaiting it. "Coming into power suddenly and in the middle of the session, they might have passed only necessary and routine measures, leaving more important bills to be prepared during the recess. No doubt the late Government would have done so, because they were never very anxious to touch home measures, and their home legislation throughout was a system of false pretences. But Mr. Gladstone had not so learned his duties and responsi- bilities, and he consequently introduced measures and vaned them which would have done very great credit indeed to any Ministry, and would have made the political fortune of Lord Beaconsfield's Government duriag the six years of its most disastrous existence. They passed a Burials Bill which he thought was generally satisfactory, except to some foolish and bigoted incumbents, one of whom, he believed, lived not very far from Warrington. They also repealed the malt tax, which had been put before the public for 40 years as a great agricultural wrong. Amongst other bills which became law was the Employers' Liability Bill, there- by putting an end to an agitation which had existed for a long time, and that in a manner which, on the whole, was satisfactory to workmen, and be believed would not be in the slightest degree injurious to the employer." These achievements alone, detached from what resulted in the cession of Dulcigno, as well as the precursory scheme de- vised for the pacification of Ireland, but which the land- owners in the Lords rendered abortive—all these labours were indeed colossal.

One is pleased to notice that, in the opinion of a great employer of labour like the member for Warrington, the Employers' Liability Bilk which on the whole, is satisfac- tory to workmen, would not be, he believed, "In the slightest degree injurious to the employer." Writing of this Liability Bill, we cannot help feeling some regret that cer- tain railway arid coal and other great trading companies seem to be using some coercive pressure to induce their workpeople to contract themselves out of Its provisions. When, some time ago, in answer to certain land measures devised for the protection of the British farmer, the land- owners were very generally found to be contriving means to contract themselves out of it, not a little contemptuous in- dignation was, and, as we think, quite just, launched at that body. To us this action of great employers appears to amount pretty much to au identical procedure. It is dis- respectful to the Legislature, whose action it stultifies ; it is a testimony of weakness on the part of the great body who have been agitating for the measure, and, to our thinking, is moreover an unfortunate course taken by great capitalists— a course in which they exhibit a contempt for law, whose sacred character no other body in the realm has a greater interest in maintaining. When we see that the agents of such a mammoth coal dealer as the Earl of Dudley are almost precipitately hustling his miners into contracting themselves out of an Act of Parliament just placed upon the Statute Book, we confess to a feeling of dismay not easily expressed.

After A vigorous and merited condemnation of the House of Lords for aggravating the condition of the Irish people, by their rejection of the Compensation for Disturbance Bill —" when the old, the halt, and the blind—particularly the blind "—hurried from all the ends of Europe to vote against the measure—Mr. McMinnies cautioned his hearers against yielding to feelings of panic or resentment. In his opinion Irish affairs were very much exaggerated, and, as a curious bit of testimony that even the Times publishes highly- coloured pictures of what it calls the anarchy of Ireland, the speaker said that he had been much struck with the statement that the Dublin correspondent of the Times—the worthy 'creature who is supposed to provide the materials for dispassionate Irish contemporary history—is no other than the editor and proprietor of the Dublin Daily Express, "one of the most foolish and violent Tory papers in , Ireland." The member for Warrington besought his hearers to place a limited faith in statements coming from such suspicious quarters, and to remember the charitable forbear- ance due to centuries of direst suffering. The speaker PrVat poet, who understood human nature, put into the mouth of a tempter of evil mese worus— Famine is in thy cheeks, refd and oppression starveth in thy eyes, Upon thy back hangs ragged misery, • The world is not thy friend, nor the world's law; The world affords no law to make thee rich. Then be not poor, but break it., And a greater than Shakespeare had told us that :whatsoever people sowed that they would also reap." Mr. McMinnies mule another notable statement. He said "He had the highest authority for saying that the leaders of the Land League did not expect to keep that con- federacy together in the face of means and measures that would bring peace and contentment to Ireland." Nor does any man expect this who understands human nature. The great measu:e of justice and pacification which the Prime Minister and his colleagues in the Cabinet will shortly sub- mit to Parliament will doubtless—with the permission of the Peers, or by-and-by without that permission—stiff the storm that frights the isle from its propriety. Whatever triumphs of peace and justice are to be achieved by the present Parliament, they will owe not e little to the Lancashire Liberals, of whom the member for Warrington is ' an admirable example. • •

Wynne Ffoulkes, Esq., Judge. • JUDGMENT BuntransEs.-- John Pemberton, -Bold, was summoned to show cause why he should not be i:orumitted to prison for disobeying an order to pay £9 13s. lid, as awarded to John Daintetk.—Mr. P. MASSEY E. SHAREsHAFT.--This was a case adjourned from last court. Judgment was now given for the defendant... DISPUTE AS TO THE QHALITIC OF GOODS.—Williana Longshaw and Sons, chemical manufacturers, Sankey Bridges, Warrington, sued the Birmingham Colour Com- pany for the sum of £ll ss. Sd., being the price of a cask of nitrate of 'lead delivered to them under their order.—Mr. Graham, solicitor, appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Moore for the defendants.—The facts of the case appeared in a mass of correspondence presented to the Court, from which it was shown that the plaintiffs wrote to the defendants offering to supply tham, with nitrate of lead at the price of £27 per ton. On the 16th of December last the defendants wrote to the plaintiffs asking for a sample to be sent, which was accordingly done and on the 18th of December, the defendants ordered from the plaintiff's five tons of nitrate of lead, as per sample and quotation, and asking for one cask to be•sent on immediately. The cask was duly forwarded by the plaintiffs, and was found by the defendants on arrival to be of a quality in- Jerior to that which they had expected from the sample shown to them. They, therefore, rejected the cask and wrote to the plaintiff, telling them that they could buy such a quality of lead elsewhere at 30s. less per ton. The cask was returned to the plaintiffs, who stated that It had been tam- pered with as the nitrate of lead sent was of a first clan quality, and unlike that sent back to them. The present action, thereupon, arose In consequence of the defendants refusing to pay for the cask. Mr. Graham, the plaintiff's solicitor, said he should prove that the quality sent to the defendants was not inferior in any. way to the sample, and that it was the custpm of the chemical trade that as soon as part of the rods were delivered, the sellers *ere entitled to t cash fourteen days after ,delivery.—Uis Honour did no think he could admit that in the face of a written document. —Mr. Graham : Then your Honour will be against me if I establish the'rules of the trade.—His Honour: Yes, on that contract. It seems to me you are suing too soon. You should have waited until the whole order was completed. —Mr. Graham: The whole of the goods have been delivered now„His Honour: You would split up one right of action into another.—Mr. Graham: Then in that case I shall be glad to withdraw the ling.—His Honour: I think it is the best way, because you are only, stung for one cask, whereas, there really are five Casks to be delivered before the ordei is completed, Then the costs, will of course, folltv the with- drawal. KNomaNG SHEEP DOWN TO THE WRONG DmoDER.— Joseph Taylor, the licensee of the Norton Arms Hotel, and an auctioneer, brought aq action to recover the sum of £ll 2s. ad. from W. Sedworth, butcher, of Cadishead.—Mr• Graham appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Wersley for the , defendant. It appeared that on the 20th of September last year, the plaintiff held one of hi a cattle sales at which the , defendant was present. A pen of sheep consigned to the sale from the farm of- Mr. Warburton, of D was put up for sale and knocked dbwn to the defendanatifloarmill 23. 6d. , The plaintiff's clerk, who was present at the time, entered the defendant's name in the sale book. as the purchaser of the flock in question, and the sheep were afterwards marked with defendant's particular sign. The defendant afterwards resisted payment of the money, and the present action was th brought to recover e amount.—The Court at this stage adjourned, and it was afterwards announced that the parties bad agreed to settle the case on payment by the defendant of £2 and costs.

NOTICE is hereby given that the PARTNERSHIP between us the undersigned JOSEPH CHRIMES and PETER CHRIMES, in the business of Brewers, heretofore car- ried on by us at the Mersey Brewery, in Warrington. in the County of Lancaster, under the firm of "JOSEPH and PETER ORRIMES," has this day been DISSOLVED by mutual consent, and that the said BUSINESS will in future be CARRIED ON by the undersigned JOSEPH CHRIMES alone on his own account, and that the said Joseph Chrimes, who is now entitled to all the partnership assets, will receive and pay all monies, debts, and liabilities owing to, or by the firm.— Dated this 31st day of December, 1880. WITNESSES W. D. JEA.1,7% JOSEPH CHRIMES. Solicitor, Wat rington. JAMES E. WORSLEY, PETER CHRIMES. Solicitor, Warrington.

ELECTION OF CORONER.—To the Free- holders of District Number 2, comprising Mints- ford, Northwich, Wkarton, Altrincham, Macclesfield, Crewe, Middiewich, Congleton, Bandbach, Buglawton, Holmes Chapel, Odd Rode, and other places in the County of Chester. Gentlemen,—Most heartily do I tender you my grate- ful thanks for the honour which you have conferred upon me by electing me to the ancient and honourable post of Coroner for this district. It shall always be my aim to merit-the confidence reposed in me by dis- charging the important duties of the office with dili- gence and efficiency. I take this opportunity of expressing to my friends who worked so earnestly to bring the contest to a suc- cessful issue, my appreciation of their efforts, and I a, k them to accept my sincere thanks. I am, gentlemen, Your obliged and obedient servant, ID C. YATES. Mean' Bank. 3lfteciesfield, 22nd December, 1880.

THE RUNCORN PROPERTY AND INVESTMENT CO., LIMITED, are prepared to receive Deposits as under :—On sums at one month's notice, 4 per cent, per annum; on sums at three months' notice, at 5 per cent, per annum. Interest payable half-yearly, on the 24th June and the 24th December. The security to investors consists of the valuable freehold estates and properties owned by the Company, proper- ties in mortgage to the Comiymy, and the large margin of un- called capital. Deposits can be paid at any time to Mr. James Pritchard, Leinster-road ; Mr. William Handley. Chu, ch- street ; and at Bethesda Schoolroom, on the first Thursday In every month, from 7-30 to 8-30 p.m,
